LONDON. Jan. Since the news
OF the discovery that the Mount Royal
was safe with all on board. dispatches
from Queenstown detail one OF the
strangest most dangerous experiences
All ocean liner has undergone within
recent years.


The Mount Royal. from Antwerp 10
ffaIifax, had almost reached her port
when she became disabled. The
steamer was at 10 degrees west long
itude, which is about $50 miles east
of Cape Race. when, battered. toss
ed, flung hither and thither by giant
waves, her machinery became disar-
ranged and her boilers began 20 leak
badly.


Mount ainous seas pounded the ship
for days. smashing time and again
clear over the bridge. The vessel
walloved. strained and plunged in in
describable fashion.


The passengers, mainly emigrants
from Southern Europe. became panic
stricken. The captain ordered them
below and the matches were battened
down.


Mad Scenes IN Steerase.


There. in the steeraee quarters. the
simple land folk. thrown violently
about the ship, believed that every in
slant the ocean would roll in and
the ship would be Swallowed up. They
prayed and raved in turn. Mothers
chung to their babes day and night,
and while families, with peasant sim
plicity, locked in embrace until ex-
hausted. fearing TO separate lest they
would die apart. Fathers and moth
ers gathered their children about them
and the most energetic and confidence
restoring actions OF the officers and
crew could do nothing To dissipate
their fears.


For days terror reigned on the ship
following Christmas eve, for il became
known that, instead of getting closer
To land, the course travelled was be-
ing retraced. Everything possible
was done To quiet the emigFants and q
constant patrol was mainland in
the steerage quarters.

NEW YORK, December 23.-Everybody
who wishes to see racing next season
will have to buy grandstand badge Or
remain outside Of the local race tracks.
There will be no field stand for the next
two years. This has been decided upon
by the Jockey Club stewards.


The Jockey Club stewards, realizing
that they will enter new era OF the
turf next season, have determined to
build from the foundation up to estab-
lish the sport. In order to build cor
rectly and to keep away from the, danger
shoals Of reform they have made the
move.


1t was the men who frequented the one
dollar Enclosure that caused the anti-bet-
ting crusade to develop. These racegoers
with small salaries and limited financial
accounts were badly crippled when they
went to the race tracks and lost their
money. AS result many families suf-
fered. Consequently there was an attack
on race track gambling which brought
about the repeal OF the Percy-Gray bet
ting law.


Another feature determined upon by the
magnates is the abolishment Of compli.
mentary tickets. Next year everybody
who attends the races will have to pay.
The only exceptions to this rule will be
the reporters who chronicle the daily rae
ing events. In former years all the poll
ticians. great and small. of this state and
city were provided with badges.

QUEBEC, July 21.-Final prepara-
tions for receiving the prince of
Wales on his arrival aboard the
battleship Indomitable tomorrow have
been made and tonight the city is on
the tiptoe of expectation. The city is
invaded by 10000 to 5,e00 soldiers, rep
resenting the regular and militia

countries, and thousands of interested
spectators from American cities and
from Canada. The city is elaborately
decorated with triumphal arches span
ming the main thoroughfares, the build
ings hung with British and French
flags and devices commemorating the
deeds Of the old French discoverers
and testifying loyalty to the royal Wis
itor, who viii come ashore tomorrow.


The Indomitable is expected about
noon tomorrow. Her appearance will
be the signal for a royal salute from
the guns OF the British battleship Ex-
mouth and the shore batteries, fol-
lowed by the combined salutes of the
international fleet of French, American
and British warships, and the answer
ing guns of the Indomitable The lat
ter viii come TO anchor alongside the
United States battleship New Hamp-
shire, thus completing a double chain
oAAioNioii VI w dISlllpS ana bringing
side by side the two latest types of
British and American fighting machine.


At Kings landing will be gathered
a distinguished party of officials to
welcome the prince, including Earl
Grey, governor general of Canada; Field
Marshal Lord Roberts. representing the
British army; Premier Laurier and his
cabinet; Admiral Jaureguiberry and the
official French envoys; Vice President
Fairbanks, representing the United
states government, and Admiral Cowles
representing the naval department.


The landing stage has been decorated
for the occasion with truly royal splen-
dor. Massive arches, emblazoned with
the arms and topped with the lion and
the unicorn guarding the British crown.
mark the passage of the prince from
the landing to the state carriage, which
viii bear him to the citadel To the
right of the landing has been erected
pavilion, richly hung with the .colors
and arms and insignia OF the refgning
family.


Here the first greetings will be ex-
changed and welcomes extended in be-
half of the imperial government of
Canada and the army. The ceremonies
concluded, the prince will drive in an
open carriage up the steep streets lead
ing from the harbor level to the
heights of the city. Along the route
the buildings are ablaze with color.
with flowers looped across the streets
and patriotic emblems and notices in
French and English expressing loyalty
and devotion to the prince.

Two brothers who had not seen each
other for sixty-four years have just
met in Los Angeles at the home of a
third brother whom they had never
seen. This proof of the oft asserted
statement that truth eXcels fiction
comes in the persons of Jacob, Austin
and John Gribling.


Fate has played peculiar part in the
lives OF these three men. The olden
painters always depicted three sisters
as the fates, and surely one sister must
have devoted much of her time to spin
ming the web of life and incidents for
each of the brothers, so complex and
strange have they been.


Remarkable Coincidence


Startling coincidence in this remark
able case is that the two who resided
in the east each wrote to the brother in
California that they intended visiting
him, writing on the same day, announc-
ing their departure on the same date,
and other plans strangely coincident
with each other, although neither one
knew that the other intended to make
the journey. The two letters announc-
ing their intended visit arrived in the
same mail.


The story of the family begins away
back in early times when Christopher
Gribling, a young man, arrived in New
York from France. He married and
settled down on a farm in Parish, N.
Y. This young man from France lived
to see six of his children, but died
shortly before his youngest child was
born.


Mrs Gribling, left with her large
family and being in moderate financial
circumstances, was compelled to sepe-
rate her numerous progeny and the
children were placed in different homes,
excepting one little girl.


There were four boys and three girls
in the family. One of the boys died a
natural death and one of the girls was
drowned by falling into, a well.


The separation of the children after
the death of the father and before the
last child was born prevented the older
from seeing the youngest


Decide to Visit Brother


Jacob, who lives in Ithaca, Mich. and
John, whose home is in Virgil: Kas,
recently decided to visit their brother
i'm California Jacob arrived two
months ago, leaving his family in the
east Had it not been that John
stopped over to visit relatives in Kan
sas he would have arrived here the
same date. He arrived here two weeks
ago with his wife, and saw his brothers
for the first time.


The brothers could not but have
recognized each other, for they look
much alike, and unknown to each other
wore their boards in the same style.


1t has come to light during these
family conclaves that Jacob and Aus
tin. who had not seen each other for
sixty-four years, had enlisted in New
York regiments and served during the
Civil War, having fought in the same
battles unknown to each other.


Austin Gribling, whom the other two
brothers are visiting, resides in cozy
home at 115 South Bright street, Whit
tier, and has a fine five-acre walnut
ranch two miles distant. He came here
five years ago from Lincoln, Neb., hay
ing been a neighbor of Bryan. The
others own valuable farms in the east


The visiting brothers will start on
their return home Monday. Jacob Crib
ling has become much enamOred of
California and expects to sell his east
ern property and move to this state.

BAKERSFIELD, Nov. 1S.-[Editor
Herald: Watching your discussions
in the Letter Box on Capitalization and
decentralization could wish more ref
erences were made to the political his
tory of this country so rich in les
sons.


From the birth of the republic this
question has split parties asunder. At
its very inception the triumphant
Wings went all to pieces over it, the
aristocratic element in the party seek
ing Capitalization and imperial power
and the Democratic element decen-
tralization and home rule.


The same quarrel between the aris-
tocrats, with their demand for special
privilege, and the peoples champions,
who opposed the Capitalization that the
aristocracy sought, ragged between the
federal and anti-federal parties. 1t

against the governmental powers that
Democratic leaders demanded for the
UNFOLDING of slavery, which then was
being fercely attacked by the Adolf
tionists, all of whom were decentrali-
cation men.


Today the Democratic, party is split
over the same question. Against the
aristocracy of money, with its lean
ings to strong government for the
protection of It's special privileges and
its special slavery, stand the people
who are victimized by those special
privileges.


Instinctively they dread the en-
croachments Of centralized power; its
growing army and navy and its grow
ing army of officials. They fear that,
as in the past, this centralized power
will be used to uphold the slavery of
special privilege.


VICTOR H. TELFORD.

CAMBRIDGE, Mass. November T.
Harvard proved Irresistible against the
Carlisle Indians today, both in the at
tack and on the defensive. and won, to
the surprise of nearly 10000 spectators,
by a score of II to q.


The result would have been several
points larger for the Crimson had it not
been for the overeagerness of the Har-
ward players when within reaching dis
lance of the Indian goal line. Four times
Harvard was on Carlisle's 5-yard line
and three times was sent back for offside
play and holding, while in the fourth in
stance her players became exhausted
from rushing and the Indians got the ball
on downs. Two minutes later Harvard
was within II yards of the Indian goal
line. but again lost the ball on downs.
1t was directly after this that the strength
of the Crimson defense was tested to the
very limit and proved unbreakable, for the
Indians were held for downs on the Grim
son o-yard line. Then came the attack
which covered practically the entire
length of the field and which resulted in
the third Crimson score. These plays
were all in the second half. In the first
half Harvard scored twice the march to
the Indian goal line starting from the
Crimson's 35-yard line, and the second
from the middle of the field.


The Indians, including the noted field
goal kicker. Balenti, proved disappoint-
ing and were never a factor in the con-
test.


Indians Look Dangerous.


Twice during the game the Indians
looked dangerous. The first time a %
yard penalty stopped their progress I'M
der the Harvard goal posts. and the sec
ond time the adamantine defense by the
Crimson stopped further progress. Ba-
lentfs only attempt at a field goal was
smothered almost before the ball left the
ground. One Harvard man, Kennard,
was ordered from the field for rough
play.


The beauty Of the modernized foot ball
was shown ably by Harvard. Three for
ward passes by the Crimson team re-
suited in long gains and two onside kicks
were carried off successfully.


1t was the Crimson's smashing on
slaught into the Indian line. however that
gained SO many yards for Harvard and
proved the feature of the game.


Indians Weak.


Harvard found the Indian line much
weaker than was anticipated, and the
Crimson backs several times tore through
for s. 10, and 10 and 20 yards. The
longest run OF the game was that by Cut
ting. around Carlisle's left end, which
netted Al yards. White made run
through center of % yards and Corbett
"a yards in his run for touchdown in
the first half.


After the loss of Kennard Harvard was
woefully weak in thu kicking department.
and arlisle'Cs chance at the Crimson goal
was due partly to McKay's inability to
boot the ball out of danger.


The first score came after fifteen min
utes of play. The ball had been going
back and forward across the field and
penalties on both sides had been frequent.
At last Harvard captured the ball on the
Crimson 35-yard line. Four rushes into
the line brought it to the center of the
field and an onside kick took it to the
Indians 24-yard line. from which point
Corbett carried it over. Then came the
first chance of the Indians to score. Get
ing the jump on the aHrvard players and
aided by a well executed forward pass,
Carlisle pushed the ball to within strik-
ing distance of the Crimson goal. but
20-yard penalty pushed the ball back,
and soon after Harvard got the ball on
downs. Then followed Harvard's sec
ond score In which the forward pass
and the onside kick were contributing
factors.

The numerous unsuccessful attempts
by the Crimson players to gather in the
4 or 5 yards between them and the
Indian goal line occupied the greater
part Of the second half. but five minutes
before the close of the game. after the
Indians exhausted themselves under the
shadow of the Harvard goal posts. there
came the great Crimson IA ~, which COW
cred the length of the field and which

NEW LONDON, Conn.,, June 25.--
Amid deafening din of whistles and
horns and amid the shouts of collie
CLANS the Harvard varsity eight shot
their boat over the finish line tonight,
winning from the crippled and dis
tanced Yale crew in that classic of
American college aquatics. the Har-
vard-Yale varsity boat race.


But instead Of a race Harvard fin
ished the last mile and half alone,
while far behind Yale limped along
with only seven men at the oars, with
Griswold, the stroke-the man who had
been relied upon to set the winning
pace-bent forward, faint from the ter
rife strain of the opening two milea


Up to this unexpected climax 1t had
been a struggle worthy of the best
traditions of the old antagonists; and
with the fitting setting of a marine
spectacle such as seldom has been
equaled along a regatta course for
brilliancy and magnitude.


For the first time, too, the president
OF the United States was taking keen
and active interest as a champion OF
the crimson colors, and although COM
PEELED by circumstances to absent him.
self today the spirit of his enthusiasm
was voiced by the Roosevelt family.
who witnessed the contest from the
deck of the presidential yacht.


Yale was more fortunate in having
her distinguished champion, Secretary
Taft. present in reality-the central
figure of group of collegians aboard
one of the observation trains. who
shouted encouragement to the Yale
crew as they sped over the early
reaches of the course and then col
lapsed into glum dismay as Griswold
was seen to fall over helplessly in the
Yale boat.


Racing Conditions Good


The race was rowed under the most
favorable racing conditions, just as
the sun was setting over the pictur-
esuue Thames, with the water broken
only by ripples, a cloudless sky and q
light northwesterly breeze The pic
ture of the straining racers as they
started on their course was one of
intense interest At either hand the
green hills of the Thames stretched
away, dotted with old fashioned New
England farm houses, the river banks
fringed with solid masses of people
and with crowded observation trains
skirting the banks and keeping abreast
of the flying boats.


The great steel bridge spanning the
Thames marked the start Of the race,
with the finish at Red Top, four miles



massed the main flotilla of pleasure
craft, with myriads of trim, white
hulled steam yachts, auxiliar!es, sloops
and schooners, the very pick of the At
lantic pleasure fleet, their rigging
bright with signal flags from stem to
stern and their sipck and span decks
alive with yachtsmen, university men
and pretty girls In bright summer Co.'S
tune, feathers, fans and gay parasols.


Further up the course, for fully four
miles, stretched long lines or steam
and sailing craft of every conceivabe
description, big ocean going revenue
cutters, torpedo boats, palatial yachts,
autoboats and sharp-beaked Herres-
hoff racers. The Sylph. with the Roose-
yelts aboard, had a point of vantage,
while all about were the racing cracks
of every class in American waters.


Through this maze of craft the racers
threaded their way with a clear open
course 200 feet wide. marked every
half mile with red and blue standards
blue for Yale and crimson for Harvard.
Every eye was riveted on the swaying
bronZed forms in the boats as they
bent to the terrific strain of 26. then
20 and then "a strokes to the minute.
driving their frail crafts through the
water as with knives. Above the shouts
from the onlookers could be heard the
shrill voices of the coxswains, mega





and marking time with "one, two,
three, four"

Harvard men had been able to take
advantage, pushing their boat slight
ly ahead. There they hung. nip and
tuck Harvard stamina against Yale
pluck, through the roaring avenues OF
nerve-racked, screeching thousands.
Half a mile from the start both crews
were almost side by side, Harvard be-
ing a few feet to the fore. One mile,
Harvard still ahead with Yale holding
on doggedly. Two miles, Yale squirting
and lessening the gap. Two and
half miles. Harvard still In the lead,
with open water between the boats
and Yale fighting on like grim death.


Now came the decisive moment, with
the final stretch almost in sight, and
the breathless throngs stratning to see
IL Harvard could keep up the pace or
would weaken at the close. Steadily,
on they came, when, suddenly, COM
motion was observed in the Yale boat,
as Griswold, the stroke, fell forward on
his oar and ceased to row.

for another effort. But they were now
six lengths behind, hopelessly beaten

The little fruit steamer Senator. from Port
Antonio. which had a terrific fight for four days
with the recent West Indian hurricane, arrived
here last night in command of her chief officer.
Captain Aarsbold, her master, having been
washed into the by a comber that broke
over the bow


The little steamer had fair weather when she
cleared Port Antonio. but when two days out the
barometer dropped suddenly and Captain Aars-
bold ordered the to prepare for storm.
He anxious to make port quickly as he
could because of the perishable cargo of fruit
he had taken on at Jamaica. When coming up
from the West Indies all fruit steamers leave
their matches open 10 give sufficient ventilation
and coolness to their fruit cargoes-


Captain Aarsbold that big storm was
coming ur and battened his matches The work
was hardly done when the hurricane kicked up
a tremendous Tons Of water pounded on
the deck and slapped with terrific force against
the house. Within half an hour after the gale
began it increased to a velocity of eighty miles
an hour, and the Senator could hardly keep on
her course.


The captain remained on the bridge through
out the first day and night Of the blow. The
steamer swung around into the trough of the sea
and was tossed furiously about from right to
left. Mountains of water crashed over the
matches and great flood poured into the hold


The pumps, however, which were in good con-
dition able to cope with the flood, and kept
the water from; putting out the fires. Cap
tain Aarsbod got his little craft out of the
trough and hoisted head sail to steady her as
she rode over the heavy seas.


When off Waiting Island, the Bahamas. the
storm threatened to carry away the SAIL and
Captain Aarsbold went forward to superintend
the work of securing it. A high rolling sea
curled over the bow and swept the captain over
board


The comber came quickly and swept aft
with such force that the unfortunate skipper had
opportunity to save himself. When the flood
cleared from the deck the captain was missing,
and il impossible to bring the steamer about
TO get him. The sea like a seething caldron,
and if the steamer had stopped instantly the
captain would have been dashed against its
sides The officers many of the steamers
which arrived here after weathering the hurri-
cane reported that no one could have lived five
minutes in the heavy seas.


The Senator continued on her course to New
York in command of her chief officer. After
losing her captain she was pounded unmerci-
fully, and two of her lifeboats smashed
into kindling wood. Eight of her vents were
also broken. Her cargo of fruit will most likely
be a total loss. because of the great amount of
water she shipped in the hurricane.

A curious and romantic story is re-
ported ffom the town of Appenzell,
Switzerland. In 1887 a Swiss, nam
ed Joseph Muller, deserted his wife
and child, little girl named Anna,
about months old, at Lucerne, and
fled to Mexico.


Nine. Muller died soon after, and
Anna was adopted by a prosperous
butcher of Lucerne, who gave the
girl good education. Eighteen
months ago the butcher sold out his
business, and bought large hotel at
Appenzell, Anna, now a handsome,
intelligent girl, managing the estab-
lishment.


Last May Joseph Muller, Annals
father, who had made large fortune
in America, arrived at the hotel, but
as Anna had taken the name of her
foster parents, he was not aware of
their relationship. A young local
doctor of good family and the elderly
Joseph Muller became suitors for
Annals hand, and in July last the girl
chose the latter.


The marriage was fixed for the end
of December, and in the meantime
Joseph Muller courted his daughter.
The day before the wedding Muller,
seeing his fiancee wearing some jew
elry which seemed familiar to him,
questioned her about it, and discov-
cred the truth. Next day he left for
Berlin, and sent his daughter letter
explaining his conduct, and advising
her to marry the young doctor, he
enclosed check for $40, 900 in the
letter.


The other day Anna Muller was
married to the doctor, but she has not
heard of her father since his flight.

by the steamer Monteagle which ar
rived this morning. The schooner Boso

Russian patrol ship arrived and seized

found the six men who had been left

deserted the schooner and took refuge
in the woods. After vain chase the
Russians returned and burned the ship.

COLOMB BECHAR Algeria. April IT,
A French column posted on Talzaza Hill
which commands the plain Of Tamlet,
was attacked fiercely at daylight yester-
day by number of Berbers, who. with
nomad Arabs. have been concentrating
for some weeks past on the western
frontier of Algeria.


Although surprised. the French force
rallied and fought desperately and not
only beat off their adversaries. but pur-
sued them for a distance of six miles. So
hot was the pursuit that the Arabs. in
their headlong fight. abandoned their
dead and wounded. Several green flags
of the prophet also fell into the hands
of the French


This French victory was costly. TWEEN
ty-cight men. including an officer. were
killed and one hundred men. including ten
officers, were wounded. The losses were
greatest in the Foreign Legion.


The Berber losses were much heavier
no less than 125 dead bodies being found
by the French troops. The French pur-
suit was stopped by darkness.

NEW YORK. Jan. 26.-Fears that an
unknown three -masted schooner and
her crew have been lost in the storm
off the Delaware capes are expressed
by officials of the steamer Mannahatta,
which limped into the harbor from Bal
timore today.


The schooner was seen struggling in
the trough of the sea off the Delaware
capes, and when the Mannahatta, which
had been blown off her course, neared
the locality where the schooner was
last sighted, riding out the storm, many
pieces of a wrecked vessel and quanti-
ties of railroad ties were seen floating
in the water.


The Italian steamer San Giovanni
reached here today with Captain H. N.
Morse and the crew of five of the oil
barge Matanzas, which, with two other
barges, the Fall River and the Grafton,
in tow of the tug Concord from Boston,
broke adrift during the storm and for
hours was at the mercy of the waves.
which wrenched off the rudder and
opened her seams. The Matanzas was
filling rapidly when the Italian mer-
chairman hove in sight and rescued
Captain Morse and his crew. The
barges Fall River and Grafton are rtill
missing.


The battered superstructures of
transatlantic liners arriving today were
mute evidence of the assaults of the
raging seas encountered during the
storm, while incoming vessels in the
coastwise and lesser trades all reported
incessant battles with the waves.

KENT. Wash. April 1O.-In a desper-
ate fight early today with five highway
men, City Marshal Miller was fatally
wounded. Night Marshal Gulberson final
ly put the robbers to flight after a hot
battle at close range. Every town near
Puget sound has been asked to keep a
lookout. and it is believed the gang will
be run down before night.


Miller received word last night that the
five men had held up and robbed Patrick
O'Brien at Orfllia. All the men were on
horseback. and they rode toward Kent
Miller and Guiberson accordingly waited
for them on the road. AS the men rode
down on them. the officers opened fire
from ambush. Their aim was poor, how
ever. for none of the outlaws were in
jured. The latter returned the fire, and
Miller fell with a bullet in his right
shoulder and another in the abdomen.


Guiberson continued the fight. He broke
from cover and ran directly toward the
men. firing all the time. His boldness
frightened the outlaws who wheeled their
horses and fled.

duel became so sanguinary that the
foam which gathered about the seal

denizens of the deep fought all after
noon and when the sun set on the scene
of battle, the dead body of the levia-
than f1oated ashore, leaving the deadly
shark master of the waters.


The day was perfectly clear and the
watchers on shore had a splendid view
of the spectacular contest, and with
glasses the details of the battle could
be followed with ease. The whale was
observed early in the afternoon by the
lookout of the life saving station, and
as he seemed to be trying to escape
from something, the most powerful
glasses were turned on him with the
result that the thrasher was discovered
in close pursuit.

cruel swordlike tail. This maneuver

terrible attacks of his relentless adyer-
sary. Apparently satisfied with his
work, the thrasher did not accompany
the body of his victim to the shore

NEW YORK, July 12.-Big crowds
on Brighton beach, Manhattan beach,
the connecting board walk and one
end of Coney island witnessed thrill
ing rescue of Charles K. Hamilton,
aeronaut, from his fallen balloon,
about mile and half out from the
shore, by the yacht Muro this after
noon. The aeronaut, who is 27 years
old and has had FIVE years experience
as an air sailor, made an ascent from
the aerodrome, Brighton Beach park,
late in the afternoon. When the bal
loon had risen about 500 feet new
sparkling apparatus with which it was
equipped got out of order. Before the
damage could be repaired the gas bag
had gone up 1000 feet, and by the
time Hamilton had pulled the cord to
release the gas strong wind had car
ried him far out over the sea.


Commodore Moran of the Muro saw
the balloonist drop with his machine
into the water and instantly ordered
his craft to attempt to reach Hamilton
DeIOre ne was pulleQ unQer the sur
face by the framework of the balloon.
Hamilton was dragged over the water
almost a mile by the partly inflated
gas bag.


Life savers set out from the beach
as Hamilton struck the water, but the
wind carried the balloon, partly sub
merged, continually away from them.
Then it was that the Muro, returning
with its owner and a party from a
trip along the New Jersey coast, ar
rived and speedily oyerhauled the fast
sinking balloon. After delicate maneu-
vering a life line was thrown to Ham
ilton and he was hauled aboard the
yacht With the balloon in tow, the
Muro then proceeded to Sheepshead
bay, where the aeronaut and the gas
bag were landed.

HONEY BROOK, Pa, July 5.-Bees
saved the little home of Miss Cynthia
Wing and prevented the kindly old
lady from going to the almshouse.


Miss Wing resides near here, and
because of her invalid state she has
had a hard time getting along. All
that she owns is a small house, with a
few acres of ground. Doctors bills
and other unusual expenses during the
last winter compelled her to borrow
money, and she gave notes for the
amount, $110


Recently she found that she was I'M
able to meet the notes and judgment
was obtained by the cruel and grasp
ing lender. He began proceedings to
sell her out and take the property.


In her woe Miss Wing wandered
about the house and finally reached
the garnet. Here she found steady
stream of bees flying In and out of a
window. The bees, she found, had es-
tablished themselves between the floors
and when she lifted loose board the
space was filled with honey.


With the assistance of several neigh
bors the flooring was taken up and the
honey collected in buckets and bar
rels. It was not of high quality but
there was about 1900 pounds of it. The
entire batch was sold for 1882.


One naturally would suppose that
Miss Wing would preserve the bees.
She did not. Instead she poured boil
ing water over them, declaring that
they Uttered up the place.

Every ship of the Atlantic fleet is
ready for the cruise around the world.
The last pound of coal was taken on
yesterday. The finishing touches to
bolt, bar and machinery have been
completed. The navy yards have done
their work and the Is ironclads are
awaiting the order to weigh anchor.


Promptly at o'clock tomorrow aft
ernoon the signal will futter from the
Connecticut and the great white ships
VIII head for the Golden gate. They
viii go out as they came in, with the
Connecticut in the van, a distance of
400 yards separating the battleships.
There will be no firing of guns.


For weeks past the preparations for
the long cruise have occupied the minds
of the officers. Full 10000 men on 10
battleships bound around the world
meant work-hard work. Flag lieu
tenants have worried themselves al
most to badness over orders, counter
orders and still more orders; chiefs of
staff have grown irritable; supply ships
have supplied and colliers dumped their
grimy necessity into the hungry bunk
ers. The engineer has petted, patted
and examined with critical eye the en-
gines.


More than 10000 men have daily
given their labors to the gigantic task.
And seated in the admirals cabin on
board the Connecticut there has been
a smiling, courteous man working
with brains. In Admiral Sperry there
was found the moving finger of the
system, the wonderful, mathematical
system which makes 5000 men single
unit.


The last auxiliary sailed Saturday
and the last battleship has taken its
place in the ranks. All day yester-
day loads of coal passed over the sides
and into the bunkers of the Ohio. Lib
erty leave for the bluejackets expired at
Z a. m today.


The ships were thrown open to the
public for the last time yesterday and
the crowds recognizing the fact
swarmed over in greater numbers than
ever.


The battleship Kansas is still in
quarantine, although the three cases Of
dipththeria have been cured and the
patients are all on the road to speedy
recovery.


Three cases of typhoid fever were dis
covered on the battleship Nebraska yes
terday. The sick men will be removed
today to the marine hospital at the
Preside.

Practically all hope Of triunion as the
proposed merging of the Congregational,
Methodist Protestant and United Brethren
churches has been termed. has now dis
appeared. Leaders among Methodist
Protestants and United Brethren blame
the Consregationalists for the failure OF
the negotiations. There was time
when union could have been accom-
plished II Congregationalists had been
willing to concede a little more, but they
asked reconsideration Of the terms OF
union which had been agreed to by their
committee. This the others were not
unwilling to grant, but II was apparent,
leaders say. that the only possible union
with the Congregational Church would
be for the other two bodies to become
Congregationalists. This they were
hardly willing to do. although negotia-
tons are still in progress.


But the great Methodist Episcopal
Church has suddenly appeared as a
rival of the Congregationalists in the
union program. The Methodist Prot.
estant. separated from the other Metho-
dist body in 1928. welcomed with open
arms the delegation from the Methodist
general conference. They were told by
the delegation that all the reasons for
the secession Of 1923 have disappeared.
One of the principal causes of the split
of that time was the refusal of the Meth
odist Church to seat lay delegates to the
conferences. But this the Methodists
have now done for years. and there seems
to leaders in both bodies to be no reason
for continued separation.


A Congregational representative also
carried greetings to the Methodist Prot
estant conference, but he was virtually
told that the Congregationalists had had
their opportunity and had lost 1t; that the
Methodist Episcopal proposition was just
now the more attractive. The United
Brethren asked whether they and the
Methodist Protestants might not come to-
gether without a third factor in the
union, and the Methodist Protestants
have suggested to them that the Metho-
dist Episcopal Church would probably
receive both. and since United Brethren
have many things in common with the
Methodist. leaders look to see this new
''triunion" methodist Episcopal, Metho-
dist Protestant and United Brethren
accomplished within a few years. Com
mittees have been appointed by all three
denominations. but their report cannot
have effect before the next Methodist
general conference, which does not meet
until 1912.

In these strenuous times the following diary

what economy woman may exercise II necessary:
An aged English lady, who recently celebrated
her nnety-second birthday, has kept from her
early days an interesting diary of her life, from
which she compiled ON her recent birthday some
curious statistics which she read out to her
assembled friends on that occasion She found,
for example, that in all her life she had used but
1000 hairpins and sixteen harnets. And in that
same period she had fortyone dresses, fortyseven
petticoats, eighty pairs of shoes and fifty-three
aprons.


AS if those facts were not enough to make her
hearers realize that economy may be practiced
by the fair sex, the widow told them that she
had used 274 pairs of stockings, 107 pairs of
garters, thirty-four shawls and wraps and sixty
three corsets. She never was extravagant in the
matter of hats and bonnets, for of those she has
purchased but 165 of both classes. With the
exception of the latter, the good lady had made
what she wore, utilizing her spare moments in
the task.


The old lady has it jotted down in black and
white that she has spent 67 100 hours in dressing
and undressing, and that she has done up and
taken down her hair 534S0 times. She has
washed her face 67,O67 times and her hands 1885,
424 times She also finds that she has slept 302,-
220 hours of her life, and drawn 1854 buckets
of water from the we'll in the back yard


She has lived chiefly on bread, cheese and milk
for the last twenty-five years.

ontinued negotiations the Indians agreed

priated for division among them. The

horna Indians and Okuma and Bentley repre-

$lO5. 600. which they will carry to their

tomorrow morning.

California have been kept busy during
the last few days burning smudges to
save their crops. 1t is not believed

injured by the prolonged cold snap.

Windsor fireman.

operations

cement wall and the loss will probably
not exceed $1,000 or $1,000. though for a
time the flames threatened to extend to

About 200 men were working in the tun-
mel when the fire broke out, and there

Despite the danger from fire, it was nee
essary to pass the men slowly through
the airlock, as they had been working

reported checked out of the shaft, how

were brought out unconscious and sent

is not considered serious

A westbound Los Angeles railway
work car jumped the track, plunged
through the railing at the side of the
First street bridge and fell on its end
to the ground, thirty feet below, short
ly before IL o'clock yesterday morning
Motorman Snyder, who had charge OF
the car, remained in the small tower
where the motor controller Is situated
and escaped uninjured.


The accident is thought to have been
caused by rotten timbers in the bridge
allowing the rails to spread when the
heavily loaded cars passed over them.


The work car was loaded with gravel
and was pushing two fiat cars also
loaded with the same material The
cars were going down the incline at
the west end of the bridgssawhen the
accident happened.


When the lower car left the rails the
coupling pin connecting it to the two
fats broke and allowed them to rush
at terrific speed down the track. Two
brakemen were riding on the runaway
cars. They applied the hand brakes
and brought the cars to stop within
short distance and before any damage
could be done.


The bridge and tracks were badly
damaged and it was several hours be-
fore repairs could be made so that
traffic could be resumed.


The bridge timbers which had been
torn up were badly decayed.

light buggy that was wildly careening
down a steep hill near Larkspur to-
day and thrown into the bushes grow
ing near the bottom OF the gulch. Ow-
ing to the lucky chance that threw the
little girl into the bush, she escaped
death and only sustained few bruises
and slight cuts about the hands and
face.


The Holmeses have been camping
near Larkspur for week. Today sew
eral children of other campers in the
vicinity began playing with light
buggy that was standing on level bit
of ground just beyond the steep de-
clivity that ends in the bottom of a
rocky gulch.


While the little Holmes girl was
playing driver the children, represent
ing themselves as horses managed in
some way to move the vehicle, and the
next moment the front wheels were
over the edge of the incline. Not rec
ognizing the danger, the children
laughingly hauled away at the shafts
until the buggy was beyond their con-
troll. With a cry of fear they dropped
the shafts and fed from the oncoming
wheels.


Little Emma, however. was helpless.
Clinging to the seat, she managed to
keep in the buggy until the shafts
struck into the roadway Then the
vehicle suddenly veered from the
straight course and the year old girl
was hurled through the air.

drowning. They are: Mrs. James Car

dragged back to the steamer by other
passengers.

Smith, who carried his baby, was Just
ahead Of his wife. She clutched the arm
of a passenger on the boat and saved
herself from falling. Her husband.
tightly clasping the baby. plunged into
the water with the other four passengers.

ported himself and his wife. but Mrs.
Carroll and her daughter. unable 10 swim,
We're foundering hopelessly and In immi-
nent danger of death

roll and she was quickly lifted to the pier
Her daughter was rescued In like manner
then Smith and his baby, followed by
Mrs Hayes and her husband, were drawn
up.


Menaced by Second Peril.


Meantime the steamboat had been work.
ing toward the pier. and it looked as IL
those in the water would be crushed

steamer at safe distance.


Mrs. Carroll and her daughter were
semi-conscious when rescued. They were
attended on the pier by a doctor from ST.
Joseph's Hospital. The others were little
the worse for their experience.


Tiny Katherine Smith, who had swal-
lowed salt water, cried necessarily until
she was in her mothers arms. Then she
cooed contentedly.

and orderly filed into the halls, filled

at the same time making way for the
numerous visitors in the building, and
went to their next period recitation

the nearly 1000 young people passing
from room to room under one roof was
silenced in a period of three minutes
after the first bells rang. The doors of
all the rooms were again closed and
the students were soon at their studies.

Saved from destruction on the seal
rocks off the Cliff house site, when her
engines broke down. the big power
schooner Newark was towed back to
port yesterday by four tiny crab fishing
bots which had rescued the vessel.


The Newark put to sea yesterday
morning bound for Byxbees. landing.
The ship had barely crossed the bar
and turned its nose out to sea when
its machinery broke down, and it be-
gan drifting toward the seal rocks.
Captain Saunders threw out both his
anchors. but neither could hold the
vessel against the tide and winds. The
vessel was being driven rapidly against
the rocks, when the four little crab
boats put to the rescue of the helpless
craft. Making their lines fast the tiny
boats got the schooner under way just
as it was about to strike on the rocks


Thousands of spectators on the
beach witnessed the rescue. and when
the little fotilla started forth with its
tow cheer went up from the specta-
tors. In this the big sea lions on
the rocks took an active interest and
Joined in the general chorus of noise.


The Newark is now lying at Lombard
street wharf.

San Diego.

drifted away from their positions.

garding the action of seven juries
which refused to enforce the law
against the separation of white and

not entitled to trial by jury any

Negroes. The litigation began
years ago when Alton established
separate schools for Negroes and
Scoot Bibb refused to send his
children to them. The late Sena-
tor John NJ. Palmer was his coun-
sci and he fought for the entry of
the Negro children to the regular
schools until his death.

SAN JOSE, Nov. 1.-Struggling des-
perately in the darkness of his guarden
shortly after o'clock this morning,
Charles Woodward. a we'll known Santa
Clara florist. had a miraculous escape
from being murdered by John Baker, a
man whom he caught prowling about
the premises. After being shot through
the calf of his leg. Baker. who is be-
lieved to be a burglar. wrenched the
loaded revolver from Woodward's
grasp. and placing the muzzle to his
breast pulled the trigger twice. Luck
lily for Woodward, the cylinder of the
weapon was loose and had turned while
the men were struggling and the firing
pin struck empty cartridges.


Foiled in his attempt, Baker pounded
Woodward over the head and face and
was only restrained from killing him
by the strenuous assistance rendered
her husband by Mrs. Woodward. Neigh
bors aroused by the disturbance held
Baker until the arrival Of a policeman.


Woodward had resolved TO protect
his extensive nursery garden from the
depredations of the small boys who
have in years past done damage in their
halloween pranks. He placed cot in
the garden and prepared to spend the
night in the open air. He fell asleep
shortly after midnight and was awak-
ened by a prowler.


The family dog located the intruder
and Woodward challenged him. The
man started to run and Woodward fired
twice into the air The man jumped
the fence and Woodward followed
Woodward fired again, this time to
make the man stop and the bullet
lodged in the calf of the fugitive's leg.


Woodward approached the man and
was grappled. His life was only saved
by the timely arrival of his wife. who
assisted in holding Baker down until
the arrival Of neighbors. Baker said
he had arrived last night from San
Francisco.

TUCSON, Ariz., July 24-In a des-
perate battle between Mexican troops
and Papago Indians Tuesday at the
Imaculada ranch, near Cetro Colorado
mining camp, in the Altar district of
Sonora, 10 Indians and two soldiers
were killed and five soldiers wounded.


The encounter resulted from an at
tempt to return the Indians to their
reservation. Usually the Papagos are
peaceful, but many complaints of dep
relations upon ranches by this band
caused the government on two previous
occasions to send troops to subdue
them.


The present expedition under Captain
Baron with so soldiers surprised an In
dian village. The soldiers found no one
in camp but two boys, as the remainder
of the population were gathering cac-
tus fruit in the hills. The soldiers set
fire to the houseS and the Indians
rushed to the rescue of their homes.


Seeing the troops, they took refuge
behind nearby rocks and opened fire.
Baron ordered the bugler to sound the
retreat. The troops retired and the
Indians pursued thinking they had
routed the soldiers. The latter, how
ever, soon halted and opened fire, kill
ing 19 of the hostiles and wounding
many.


The Indians fed, taking their wound
ed with them. Among the killed are
Chief Dolores and his son. These two
are said to have been the chief trouble
makers. The Wounded soldiers were
taken to Hermosillo.

IRVINE, Ky, Dec. 26.-The jurors In
the case of Beach Hargis, charged with
the murder of his father. Judge James
]. Hargis reported their inability to
agree this afternoon and were dis
charged. The jury stood nine for ac-
ouittal and three for conviction.


Beach Hargis had been on a debauch
a few days before the time OF the
murder of Judge Hargis and he hnaily
had been brought back to jackson.
For some days the neighbors declared
that Judge Hargis had been dragging
the boy through the streets OF the
wild little mountain town.


Beach entered his fathers store and,
after a few words with the judge,
grappled with him. They fell to the
floor, Beach on top, and with the judges
own pistol the boy fired several shots
into the body of the prostrate man.
MOTHER DEFENDS PATRICIDE


The defendants mother testified that
the Judge had taught the boy bad
habits, and when Beach was a child
had given him whisky and buckled
gun on his hip. Beach, or Beauchamp,
his rightful name, is % years old and
has already been what in the Kentucky
mountains is termed "feverish.


Judge Hargis was admittedly baron
in Breathitt county, and even in the
tenth congressional district as auto
cratic as a medieval lord. His min
listers occupied all the county offices,
he was himself democratic committee
man and was chairman of the district
conventions.


Men rose up to question his rule and
to make personal attacks on him, and
these men suddenly were done away
with.


VIOLENT RULE CAUSED MURDERS


The Marcums. the head of which
family walked the streets of Jackson
for months with a baby in his arms
10 avert his final assassination; the
Cockrills and others disputed the scepter
of the feudal king and paid the pen
atty with their lives. This summary
and violent rule bred the school of
murderers and bad men who gave to
their county the world known title of
Bloody Breathitt." One of them, Curt
Jett, called by his picturesquely speak
ing neighbors the wild dog of Breath
itt' is serving a life sentence; some
are dead and others have fed the state
or are living quietly since the death
of their chieftain.


Hargis had vast mineral interests in
this section, on which he lived though
the ostensible producer of his wealth

SOHlSu uiNlSlon 4 OF the DaLtleSHlp 1leel
Sunday morning, the sun smiling q
California welcome on the floating
fortresses and the Santa Monica bay
pcpulace backing up the sunny well
come with more substantial one.


The four splendid battleships, Maine
(hagship), Ohio, Missouri and Mime
sofa steamed majestically into the
broad expanse of water at $3.50, con-
tlnued to the northern end, then turned
round and distributed itself between
Pier avenue, Santa Monica, and the
breakwater at Venice.


Captain G. b. Harber, In command
of the Maine, commands the division
this being the quartet of battlers OF
which Admiral Thomas had command
before Admiral Evans became inva-
lded. When Thomas was in charge
there the Minnesota was the flagship.
Santa Monica bay, noted for its
marine panorama, never bore a more
formidable, ponderous or historic quar-
tet of warships than yesterday, and
her people, augmented by Los Angeles
Visitors, did all that human endeavor
could to let the crews know that they
realize that ''our division had come"


Their First Glimpse


Thousands Of those on shore doubt
less helped to swell the throng be-
tween San Pedro and Newport bay to
note the entry of the squadrons Sat
urday, but many thousands more
caught their first glimpse of the At
lantic fleet yesterday and to all IT was
a memorable occasion.


After the entry into the bay the
women of the cities adjacent boarded
the warshps and distributed boutton-
ieres for every man aboard. Each one
surrendered instantly and submitted to
having the flowers pinned to his coat
or blouse.


This pretty ceremony, performed by
100 young women--twenty-five for each
battleship-served as the formal well
come, though mayors of Ocean Bark
and Santa Monica and staffs shook
hands with the officers and spoke cor
dial words of greeting.


Easter Sunday opened perfect day.
The sun shone its most balmy way,
the hillsides and the beach contrasted
in perfect harmony. light wind blew
yet did not ruffie the sea, and as soon
as the electric car service began the
beach and piers began filling up with
happy humanity with outstretched
hands for the boys in blue.


Hour after hour the throngs swelled,
for the early visitors came particularly
to see the incoming of the division.


On Easter Morn


A few minutes after o'clock the
flagship Maine, whose coming called
up memories of its Inflated predecessor,
hove into sight, and stately, terrible
and silent, led the way to the ocean 8
expanse. The moment the head of the
line appeared automobile horns sound
ed people cheered, handkerchiefs
waved and all the boats equipped with
noise makers were heard. There are
no factory whistles near the shore
line.


With the perfect alignment and dis
position as to space that has all along
marked the progress of the great fleet
the white and dun colored ships OF
peace proceeded northward as though
heading for the long wharf at Port
Los Angeles. Then the signal nags
began to flap and change and the flag
ship slowly described an arc and turned
back to the south. The division had
held its dress parade and was pro-
ceeding to It's anchorages.


AT slower speed the turn was made,
the flagship increasing its distance and
the last ship, the Minnesota, appar-
emily slowing down. The maneuver
then became apparent. The captains
were spreading their proud ships over
an aera extending from Venice to
Santa Monica.


Anchors Splash simultaneously.


For an instant it seemed the big
battlers halted, then there came a
splash and simultaneously four great
forward anchors slipped to the oceans
tottom with a splash that sent up
miniature waterspouts.


For a little while only they lay
broadside to the beach. Then by tidal
action the craft swung around on their
chains and directly their sterns point
ed to shore. In this position they re-
manned.


The first anchorage was in a line
about a mile from shore. This seemed
to the committee a bit too far, as 1t
reduced the carrying capacity Of the
launches by lengthening the running
time. Only nine out of the forty boats
had reported for duty and short hauls
were imperative.


Captain Harber, therefore. at 10
o'clock ordered the anchors weighed
and changed the divisional position,
moving. 200 yards nearer shore.


This move was welcome, but it con-
sumed an hour and a half and re-
duced the number of persons who were
able to visit the four battleships in
proportion.


The first boats which left the bat
tleship fleet for shore had orders to
convey the hundred committee women
who bore Easter flowers for the sailors.
They had the right of way. 1t was
Southern California's Easter greeting
to the men of the fourth division


At Femlninlty's Feet


The young women were garbed in
their gayest clothes and Easter hats,
their eyes and smiles were brightest
and patriotism had no prettier expon-
ents than the Santa Monica bay COM
mittee bearing garlands and blooms for
the boys in blue.


They were received with due dig
nifty, twenty-five to each warship, and
then given the freedom of the decks,
the men being drawn up in line for the
floral ceremonies. smile and kind
word went with each couttoniere as it
was pinned on each --lanly breast,
forthwith putting the wearer meta
phorically at the feet of the fair ones.
Then in groups the officers invited
the visitors to inspect the ships and
femininity did so from the fighting
tops to the engine rooms. The escort
ing officers aver that they never had
better listeners, more intelligent audi
ences or more enthusiastic girls than
the fair one hundred.


When the last of the fair ones
stepped down to the landing stages
tne order was given to change anchor
age and in few minutes huge volumes
of smoke shot out of the tunnels. Di-
rectly the anchors were lifted and the
division moved closer to hospitable
shores. 1t is said today the four ships
may move still nearer the pier.

their work and toward herself. She
approached quite near and acted as If
lame and distressed. She would lie
down on her side and writhe along the
ground. uttering whines and means.
Then she would limp off, going slowly
and frequently.


The hunters We're not to be drawn
away from the work in hand by such
tactics, and finally, after much digging,
came upon the den, where the five little
fellows were shrinking. Maine hunters
say it is unusual for mother foxes to
leave all their young in one place. 1t
is their cunning habit to scatter the
family in widely separated retreats.

banks, Frank Marks, Strongyille farmer,
converted all his money into gold coin and
hid the metal under the floor Of his pig
pen. While he and his wife were in Cleve


land robbers searched his house, ripping
mating and upholstery in an effort to To-
cate the hidden wealth. Incidentally the
thieves fired the barn and pig pen. Neigh
bors fought the flames and saved the
house. Upon his return home Marks sur
prised his friends by digging in the ruins
of the pig pen and drawing forth huge
lump of gold said to be worth several
thousand dollars The gold coins had

effect of prosperity on character Mrs.
Humphry, a prominent social writer,
declaims against the alleged brutaliz-
ing influence of wealth on American
women.


She tells of an American girl in Lon
don who was starving, but desperate
and deserving, and whose case she
brought to the notice of two wealthy
American women residents here. They
ignored the matter.


"There they are" says Mrs. Hum
phry, "wallowing in their wealth and
letting a poor little compatriot suffer
all the miseries of poverty, including
bitterest despair. But for other kind
err English friends she might have
committed suicide. She is now rescued
from her desperate position and, being
clever, will probably make her own
way.


"Wealth In many cases ruins the dis
position of those who have not pre-
viously known the correcting influence
of poverty. They become hard and
brutal.

LONDON. September 26.-The stock ex-
change has had a fairly active week S
trading with generally steady under
tone, and in spite of the early break In
American securities quotations on British
shares foreigners and kaffirs showed
fractional advances. Gilt edge shares,
especially the good yielding securities,
were fortified by the investment of the
banking balances and the funds released
from trade channels and rose toward the
week end while better traffic returns, to-
gether with reports of further pooling
arrangements strengthened home rails.
although the cotton crisis checked pro-
nounced upward movement.


The American section provided the most
interest and excitement during the week.
Prices jumped about in erratic man
ner The slump early in the week created
anxiety about the differences to be met
in the forthcoming settlement. but the
market later gave an exhibition of re-
markable recuperative powers under per
sistent support from the other side. This
induced Berlin and Amsterdam houses to
cover their earlier sales. the result being
a rise in the leading stocks of from three
to six points from the lowest. The final
values were within one point of last Sat
urday's close. Some realiZatiOns today.
however, gave the market rather I'M
settled appearance. Union Pacific closed
three points lower than last Saturday.

a decision to-day in the case Of the collision
between the cruiser Gladiator and the
American liner St. Paul said he would
render judgment merely as between ship and
ship apart from any individual action by
those on board the Gladiator.

was not excessive. that 1t was not true that
her helm was starboarded. but that her
maneuvres were substantially as pleaded by
her owners and that the Gladiator was dis
tinctly to blame.

who had asserted that the st. Paul gave a
two blast signal were mistaken. There
was only one blast. There would have been
no collision If the Gladiator's helm had not
been improperly starboarded.

ZEIGLER, ILL.,, December 21.-With e
stubborn fire slowly fighting back hun
dreds of men who have been ceaselessly
at work for days seeking to save the Goa
supply of the great Zeigler mine, Joe Lei.
ter. Chicago millionaire, and his beautiful
young wife have joined forces with the
workmen and are personally comba ting
the flames. Early today Letter and his
wife, formerly Miss Juliette Williams OF
Washington, D. c., were at the scene oi
the conflict. Letter was leading the work
men with an inspiring energy, while on
the fighting line. tired but determined
was his beautiful young wife. serving the
almost exhausted men with coffee and
sandwiches and encouraging them by hel

firefighter, singed by the heat. overcome

ton, was brought out of the shaft he

STA. Powhattan. Laisang, Charles Har-

ing are ashore. An unknown steamer and

blocked by debris. The British steamer

typhoon and each sustained considerable
damage above the water line.


Much Property Damage.


MANILA. P. l.. Jily 2s.-A destructive
typhoon swept over Hongkong at mid
night last night, causing heavy loss of
life among the Chinese residents and un-
roofing many buildings. The typhoon
caused tempestuous seas which resulted In
several steamers being driven ashore.


Among the buildings damaged were the
offices of the Pacific Mail Steamship Com
pany and'the Kingsclere Hotel. The for
mer buildings collapsed completely, while
portions of the latter crumbled to the
earth from the force of the hurricane.


There was no loss of life reported among
the foreign nha bitants.


The British steamers Persia and Schuyl-
kill and the coasting steamers Charles
Hardouin and Lai Sang were battered
against the shore, where, at last reports,
they were still resting.


Gallant Work, This.


The crew of the British cruiser Astraea
performed gallant service in attempting
to rescue the Chinese crew of a derelict
junk. After battling desperately in the
mountainous seas for an hour the Brit
ishers succeeded in rescuing six out of a
total of thirteen. The remaining seven
were drowned The property loss on shore
will be heavy

The steamer Admiral Schley, of the United
Fruit Company, arrived here last night from
Port Antonio with the captain and crew of the
burned schooner Lulie l. Pollard who were
literally snatched from the Jaws of death IN a
heavy gale and high sea 2T2 miles southeast
of Sandy Hook at o'clock on Saturday even
ing


The Schley was on time and 1t was due to her
consistent run up the coast that she was able to
drag off from the blazing schooner the captain
and five men, who an hour later would have
been burned to death drowned in the heavy
sea.


Captain ]. c. Powell of the Pollard and his
men said last night arrival that they thanked
God and the captain and men on the Schley for
their escape from death.


The little three master left Charleston 8 c.
on Octoder 26 with lumber ty phiia i'hia
She took her cargo at Fernandina, Fla. on Oc-
tober 10 but was driven by terrific gales to
seek shelter in Charleston on October II. She
nut out again on October %. and was on her
way up the coast to Philadelphia when the
cook struck match near some pine boards
soaked with resin, and before any one aboard
could check ii a blaze crept along the cargo
to a small house amidships sheltering two tanks
of gasolene the fuel for hosting engine


The flames woke up the men off watch, and
every one aboard except the man at the wheel
buckIed to in a desperate battle for MS ne
The course OF the schooner was changed to keep
the wind from blowing the fire TO the tanks but
without avail The mate, who ran toward the
tankhouse with a handful Of wet sacks, forced
his way through The flames just as they struck
the tanks. and he and the cook, who was behind
him. were hurled ten feet aft along the deck.
They fell in such q way that they escaped In
Jury and were ready. within a few minutes
after the shock to renew their fight with the
fire.


high wind carried cinders forward. and
within ten minutes the forward section was
cracking. The men on the Pollard said last
night that the ship as hot as roaring fur
mace. and that their only hope of saving them
selves depended on their ability to dodge the
flames that shot about in all directions.


Seeing that there was chance to save their
clothing and effects forward the men huddled
aft and tried to isolate themselves from fire by
throwing buckets OF water before them. Their
courage almost failed whcn they saw two life
boats forward consumed by the flames, and their
one thought from that time was to save the
Hfeboat aft, which they shifted from its Chocks
and swung over the stern. where the Combers
could keep it wet.


There was a heavy sea running, but even the
occasional breaking OF comber on the deck
forward was insufficient to check the in



owner Of the little schooner. stood with his men
cool and calm although he realized that his own
property was being destroyed before his eyes
and that the lives of his crew well as his own
were mighty poor insurance investments. There
was a hurried consultation and the men agreed
to huddle up on the stern until the heat should
force them to leave the schooner The wind
was from the northeast, cold and penetrating.
but the heat from the burning pine cargo made
the air hotter than that In the tropics.


Captain Powell said minutes seemed like
hours In their terror the crew Of the Pollard
scanned the horizon for a steamer. They were
close to the northbound coastwise track. and
hoped they would be able to hang 70 the burn
ing schooner until help arrived. In the excite
ment thev did not notice that the Admiral
Schley. northbound, bearing down on them
at top speed.


Captain Jensen Of the fruit steamer saw the
Pollard long before the schooners crew noticed
the smoke from the Schey's funnel The smoke
from the burning cargo rose high in the air, and
Captain Jensen realized that the Pollard was in
q bad way. He changed his course and ordered
the engineer to push the Schley at top speed.
Within forty-fve minutes after the schooners
cook had lighted the fatal match the Schcy
was cicse by, and without waiting for the Pol
lard to signal that she needed assistance, Cap
tain Jensen had a llfeboat lowered and under
way through the heavy to the helpless men
on the schooner


The men. who had put on cork jackets when
they saw that nothing could save the Pollard.
Jumped into the and were picked up by the
lifeboat from the Schley Captain Powell was
the last person to leave HIS burning craft. He
and his men were provided with clean clothing
and were supplied with stimulants and food.

Twelve thousand Germans, imbued
with the festival spirit. trooped through
the gates of Shell Mound park yester-
day to celebrate the two hundred and
twenty-fifth anniversary of the first
landing OF Germans under Pastorius
at Germantown, Pa. 1t was far and
away the largest crowd that has con-
son and in point of enthusiasm broke
all records. Eighty-six German So
cieties were represented and Of these
21 had booths.


The festivities started early in the
day and were continued till dusk, dane
ing. bowling and divers other games
keeping up the interest OF the multi
tude.


The principal speeches of the day
were made by John Hermann, president
of the German league of California, and
William Erythropel, German vice-con-
sui. Both orators referred to the cor
dial feeling existing between the United
States and the fatherland. and exhorted
their listeners to promote continuance
of this good will. Consul General Bopp,
who is at present absent on furlough,
sent cablegram from Naples. wishing
the gathering much pleasure and pre-
dieting success for the German So
cieties of California


Two of the most interesting features
of the day were the exhibition of the
turner vereins and the singing of the
saengerbund. The Turner's were repre-
sented by four organizations, the San
Francisco, Oakland, Mission and Elm
tracht vereins- The singing was under
the direction of Professor Riegger and
about 200 voices composed the chorus.
The old chorus entitled 20 Wald Nit
Deinen Duff Gen zweigen" was the
favorite with the audience.


During the day subscriptions were
received amounting to $1,000 for the
proposed German house which will be
erected in San Francisco.

BY Associated Press


SAN FRANCISCO. Aug. 2.-The
three surviving victims of the automo.
tains yesterday, in which Mrs. Fred
erick Marriott and Jesse Gilbert, who
was acting as chauffeur, met death, ar
river here today.


Miss Dorothy Partridge, although
badly burned, is getting along well,
and unless blood poisoning develops
will recover. Miss Desire Marriott,
aged years, is suffering from a badly
injured nose, and was otherwise cut
and bruised. Frederick Marriott, pro-
prietor of the News Letter, was bruised
and is suffering from shock.


Marriott attributes the accident to
narrow and poorly constructed road
on the summit of the Santa Cruz noun
tains. Gilbert was at the wheel and
the car was going at a good speed
down the grade. about ten miles from
Los Gatos. Suddenly the soft earth on
the side of the road gave way and the
heavy machine plunged down an en-
bankment turning over twice before
1t struck against a tree.


Mrs Marriott was caught under the
tonneau and killed instantly, her neck
being broken. Gilbert lived only
three minutes, being suffocated under
the car.


When Miss Partridge, who was on
the front seat alongside Gilbert, real
lied the car was going over the en-
bankment, she tried to jump, but Gill
bert seized her wrist and held her
tight. She, too, was caught under the
automobile and remained there an
hour and a half, suffering great agony
from burning gasoline and hot water
which fell from the machine. When
the unfortunate young woman was
finally released Gilbert's hand still
held her wrist in the grasp of death.


Desire Marriott was pinned under the
car, but was quickly rescued by her
father, who had been thrown free from
the wreck.


Turns to Work of Rescue


Marriott picked up a jack and lever
as he struck the road, and Immediately
set to work to raise the car and re-
lease the others. He was horrif1ed to
find his wife and Gilbert dead, and,
but, though himself badly bruised,
worked rapidly to save his daughter
and Miss Partridge.


After releasing his daughter and do
ing what he could to alleviate the suf-
fering of Miss Partridge, Marriott
walked to a neighboring farmhouse and
telephoned for medical and other assist
ance.


Only five minutes before the accident
occurred Mrs. Marriott had exchanged
seats with Miss Partridge, entering the
tonneau with her husband and daugh-
ter, allowing their guest to take the
front seat.


AS the car went down the embank-
ment Miss Partridge fell to the bot
tom, and to this she probably owes her
life.


The remains of Mrs. Marriott and
Gilbert are to be brought here and
will be cremated. Gilbert was
a close friend of the Marriott family
and had Travelled extensively with Mar
riott, jr., who was in Los Angeles with |
his wife when the tragedy occurred

nese, Jung Jow and Mock Kung. will be

Since their conviction the two men

The condemned men were members of

their defense was furnished by a levy
made on the membership of that organi-
Zation.


Met Death StoicallyA


Both men went to their death stoically
and neither uttered a word after lea wing
the cell. The hanging was expeditiously
done. only two minutes having ELAPSED
from the time the sheriffs party left the
prison clerks office to the springing of
the trap. The murderers were pronounced
dead fifteen minutes later.


Jung Jow and Mock Kung died in the
Christian faith Some weeks ago they
became Baptists and Baptist clergyman
remained with them up to the moment
they mounted the gallows. The Rev Lee
Hung of the Philadelphia Baptist Chi
nese Mission took charge of the bodies

Philadelphia. March 2.-Before the next
Army-Navy football game shall bring
tens Of thousands hocking to Philadel-
phia from all parts OF the East, it is the
wish Of naval men that a vast temporary
stadium will rise from the spreading
acres Of League Island Navy Yard. and
that the great contest will be waged there
under government auspices.


For five years army and navy officials
and the athletic associations OF West
Point and Annapolis have struggled with
the problem Of providing adequate ac-
commodation for the crowds which flock
to the game, to find a location geographi-
caIy suitable. and to realize for the army
land navy purposes. philanthropic and
athletic, some of the financial return in
evitable when all the world wants to see


Game Is I'm Demand.


Every possible solution has been con-
sidered Princeton offered terms which
promised some Of the financial reward,
but the Inconvenience imposed made the
experiment disastrous, and it will never
be repeated. Every city and every great
university Of the East would welcome the
army and navy. but geographical consid-
erations have pointed to Philadelphia as
the scene of the contest Heretofore
Philadelphia has meant Franklin Field.
There is prospect now that PENIS IA
nous battle-ground will not again boast
the official. social. and athletic distinction
which it has enjoyed in the past. but that
Philadelphia, still host OF the football
heroes, will journey southwark TO the
navy yard and not across the Walnut
street bridge.


Al a stroke this move would accomplish
ali that has been desired by both Army
and Navy. The game would be played
exclusively under government auspices
there would be no division of tickets with
a third institution. Whatever financial
return there might be would be at the
disposal of West Point and Annapolis
the geographical center would be pre-
served but most important, accommoda-
ton could be provided for the last Army
or Navy enthusiast who might desire
70 see the crowning event OF the Ameri-
can athletic year.


Expense No Drawback.


League Island has the acres. Tempo
rary stands would prove costly. but q
single years returns would wipe out
this cost and leave margin beside. while
even temporary stands would answer the
purpose for several successive years, and
could be paid for ten times over before
new ones would be needed. League
Island to-day is not so accessible foI
street car transportation as Franklin
Field. There are possibilities for railroad
track extensions and street cars and
special trains together might readily
carry the crowd.


Navy enthusiasts explain away every
possible objection, and Il is said thai
the feasibility Of the project has inn
pressed men high in both branches oi
the service. Campaigning with this enc
in view viii continue throughout tht
summer, and next fan will probably find
the carpenter and builder at work.

imploring him 10 tell the nature ana
seriousness of the accident. Every ef-
fort was made to quiet the frightened
persons, but the intense excitement did
not subside until the steamer started
once more on her way.

believed that the detached propeller
drove a hole in the steamers bottom.

sandy hook, at the gateway OF New

She of the far-famed empty cupboard

There came knocking upon the door.
And as she fastened across the floor

1t nearly took away her breath
And frightened her almost half to death.
There were people here, there were people there

board!"

Dame Trot and all the endless crew
That lived together in shoe,
And many another known to fame
Had but room to give his name.
This much to tell you will suffice
They each and all brought something nice
To fill the cupboard o'er and DER.
In fact, their gifts bestrewed the floor.
On every chair and table stood
Some article of daily food.
Each nook and corner held a dish
OF either food or flesh or fish
Till Mother Hubbard scarce could find
A resting place for foot or mind,
While doggie walked on his hind legs
For fear of breaking pies or eggs.
And, as for all the company,
They had to stand outside, you see.
Yet, as they had to leave quite soon
To see the COW jump DER the moon,

But what about the sumptuous feast
Inside the cottage? Must tell
The fearful ending that befell
The hungry dog who ate and ato
And brought about the cruel fate
1t is my duty to relate?
For he, who lived upon bone,
Died when with plenty left alone,
And ere the morning stars grew dim
He stiffened out in every limb.
So Mother Hubbard buried him.

Some people are thrown off theil
balance the moment anything goe:
wrong with them. They do not seen
to have the ability to overcome imped.
iments and to do their work In spite
of annoyances.


Anybody can work when every
thing goes smoothly, when there Is
nothing to trouble him; but mar
must be made of the right stuff who
can rise above the things that annoy,
harass, and handicap the weak, and
do his work in spite of them. In
deed, this is the test Of greatness.


AS a matter of fact, the greatest
achievements In all time have been
accomplished by men and women who
have been handicapped, annoyed, per-
secuted, misunderstood, critized. But
they have been great enough to rise
above all these things and to do their
work in spite of them.


Few people are large enough to rise
above their aches and pains and disap-
pointments. The majority always
talking about them, projecting their
dark shadows into your atmosphere,
cutting off your sunshine with their
clouds. Their ailments and their
hard luck and misfortunes seem to be
the biggest things about them. You
never meet them but they thrust them
into your presence.


The man who is not big enough to
rise above things that trouble him,
who can not overtop his aches and
pains, annoyances and disappoint-
ments, SO that they are of little con-
sequence in comparison with his great
life aim, will never amount to much.


There is an unwritten law for peo-
pie who are thoroughbred-the real
gentleman and the real lady-which
compels them to keep their troubles,
their ailments, their sorrows, their
worries, their losses, to themselves.
There is a fine discipline in it. 1t
mellows the character and sweetens
the life. But when these things are
not borne heroically, they mar the
character and leave their ugly traces
in the face, their hideous forms appear
in the manner and disfgure the whole
life.


Learn to consume your own smoke.
If you have misfortunes, pains, dis
eases, losses, keep them to yourself.
Bury them. Those who know you
have them will love you and admire
you infinitely more for this suppress
sion. A stout heart and persistent
cheerfulness will be more than match
for all your troubles.-Swccess.

about 300

By following the wreckage Of towns the gen
eral direction OF the tornadoes be traced
closely. Apparently the struck in three
separate currents. each describing the arc OF
circle and travelling toward the northeast. The
first Of these struck through Northern Louis
lana, Mississippi and into Tennessee before day
light Friday morning. The second appeared fur
Their south about o'clock in Central Louisiana

and Georgia Friday night and Saturday

peared Friday afternoon. further south than

Why the fatalities were so large is apparent

have arrived here from many portions Of the

Whole blocks Of what were formerly little resi-
dences and cabins. lie spread over the ground in
separate boards, if huge lumber pile had

mass of wreckase many hundreds Of persons

injured

horseback have gone through country districts.

dering aid where it was most necessary. At

DECKERV1LLE. Mich, July 22.-Thir-
teen men were rescued from the burning
deck Of the steamer Charles A Street on
Lake Huron Monday night through the
heroism Of Capt. Noah Forton Of the
barge Godfrey, and his crew.


The Streets engineer discovered the fire
In the stern Of the boat shortly after II
o'clock. 1t spread SO rapidly that though
the crew fought the flames stubbornly
the men were driven back. The interior
OF the hull was a raging furnace and the
flames were speedily devouring the upper
works In the forward part of the boat.
The ifeboats were burned away and the
crew was without means Of leaving the
doomed vessel.


The Street was toying three barges,
but when the fire started on the steamer
the towline was parted and the burning
boat drifted away from the barges. Capt.
w. r. Dunn Of Detroit. in command Of
the Street, ordered the crew to prepare
life RATS. With the flames licking the
woodwork on the deck a. few feet from
them, the members of the crew worked
rails and upper works and trying to lash
them together to form a raft.


Meanwhile Capt. Forton Of the barge
Godfrey, the last in limo, ordered the
barge's boats out. For three miles the
crews pulled the lifeboats. which were
tossed around like corks. TLey reached
the side of the burning steamer in an
exhausted condition. The crew of the
Street clambered into the small boats and
rowed their rescuers away. All were ex-
hausted when they reached the barge.
