Hurrying westward on a train, the
mother of little Mary Preston will be
shocked to learn that her child is at
the county hospital, recovering from a
bad fall she sustained Monday after
noon.


1t was while dreaming of her mother
that she fell, and by sheer good luck
and quick medical attention alone did
she escape with her life.


Little Mary awoke after a 20-foot fall,
sorely injured, to find herself in the
arms of DR.. Adolph Peter. Sympathiz-
ing friends stood near, fearing that life
had left her. She tunbled off the rear
balcony of Hotel Alton, at 533 South
Spring street, and landed in a heap
after grazing dry goods box in the
yard below. The collision with the box
dislocated the child's vertebrate at the
neck, and but for immediate medical
aid she would have lived only a few
moments.


DR.. Peter placed his knee against the
child, gave her a jerk, and with snap
the delicate bones slipped back into
place. The spinal system had been in
jured, but the doctor said the effects
would pass away quickly. The child's
arm was fractured and she also sus-
tanned severe Commissions of the head.


Her grandmother, in whose care she
has been for some weeks, having pre-
ceded her mother to the coast, Is with
the patient constantly at the hospital.
Guests at the hotel send flowers and
fruits at intervals.


Both grandmother and child watch
the door of the ward expectantly, as
the mothers presence is expected hour
ly. She left New York a week ago. AS
it is not known which route she is
travelling over no dispatch has been
sent her.


1t appears that the girl fell asleep
while seated on an iron stairway lead
ing from the balcony. She had been
attracted by the music coming from
the monograph establishment down.
stairs, and, as she often did, sat there
a long time holding her Teddy bear
and listening to the melody.


Mary told her grandmother when she
recovered consciousness that she had
had the sweetest dream, in which she
saw her mother coming to kiss her.
She stretched out her arms, and the
next moment all was blank That was
when she struck terra f1rma.


The doctors say the little girl who so
luckily escaped will be out in a week.
They give Dr. Peter credit for saving
the girls life by prompt treatment.
The rear of his Office and the yard
where the girl fell are only few feet
apart. Hence his prompt presence.

From the New York Sun.


A few natives of the Caroline Islands
have again answered the old conundrum
how the widespread islands of the Pacific
came by the people who were found on
them. The Caroline Islanders are born
Seamen and no mariner who knows their
skill and daring will be surprised TO
hear that in March last year six of them
confidently put to sea to visit Japan-oyer
200 miles away.


They were out less than a week when
the terrible typhoon that in four days
brought complete destruction to some of
the islands wrecked the little vessel. She
still foated. but had no rudder. mast
sails oars. The men aboard her were
helplessly adrift.


For two months they saw nothing but
the heavens and the sea, till one night
a light Shone out. but the caStawayS
feared unfriendly natives and did not
try to reach the light. though that very
day their last bit of food had been eaten.


They caught fish and turned their pro-
vision boxes into firewood 10 cook them.
They partly assuaged thirst by spreading
their garments to catch the rain. So on
they drifted. half dead, and no one knows
exactly how long, for the time was not
recorded. when they were pulled out OF
their boat on the shore of North Formosa.
All but one were senseleSs; two died in
few hours and the others recovered. The
distance between their starting and land
ing points is LOO miles.


Some years ago all the records of drifts
long sea journeys of Pacific islanders
were collected and this mass of evidence
left practically no doubt that the myriad
islands were populated by such voluntary
or Involuntary wanderings.

DEER LODGE. Mont. March o.
Warden Frank Conley Of the Montana
penitentiary was severely wounded yester'
day and Assistant Warden John Robinson
was killed by three life convicts. George
Rock, w. H. Hayes and another, who
tried to escape. Robinsons throat was
cut from ear to ear. and the jugular vein
was severed. Conley's throat was gashed
and he was stabbed several times In the
shoulder and the groin before he was able
to draw his revolver and shoot down
Hayes and Rock, who were armed with
pocket knives. 1t is believed that the
warden will recover.


The three convicts were taken to the
Office Of the penitentiary by Deputy
Warden Robinson to be tried before War
den Conley for some infraction Of the
prison rules. Hayes had for several
months been a rusty and served Is
cell with Rock, who had been regarded
as desperate man. The moment the men
entered the ONCE Rock turned swiftly on
Robinson, who was closing the door be-
hind the men, and quickly drawing knife
slashed the deputy warden's throat SO
deeply that Robinson fell helpless and
soon died


At the same moment that Rock attacked
Robinson Hayes drew knife and started
for Conley, who retreated to the rear OF





revolver Hayes had sprung on the war.
den and slashed his throat from the left
ear to point under the chin. Conley halt
eluded the blow and struggled desperately
Hayes, seeing his intended victim getting
away, stabbed the warden several times
in the shoulder and the groin.


Although bleeding terribly, Conley man.
aged to draw revolver and fire four
times. with the weapon pressed against
Hayes abdomen AS Hayes sank to the
moor Rock rushed at Conley, who fired
the remaining bullet into Rock. and the
latter fell helpless.


The third convict took to his heels at
the beginning of the throat-cutting, but
he was quickly captured. The prison
of1cers refused to give out the name until
they have investigated whether he was
concerned in the plot.


How Hayes and Rock got the knives
Is not known. II Is believed that the
1nfraction of the rules had been planned
in order to reach the warden's Office,
whence the convicts would have a better
chance to escape, once the warden and
his deputy were out of the way.

The first firing commenced at $3.50
o'clock and was the slow fire at the
200-yard target, which soon was com
pleted. This was followed by shooting

first half was completed. While some

open boat on a storm-swept ocean, Capt
Charles F. Hines and the crew of seven
men of the Baltimore schooner John A.
Mathesen were brought into this port
today on the steamer Seminole, returning
from Santo Domingo.


Capt Hines, in telling his story OF the
disaster, said that the sMathesen sailed
from Baltimore August % with cargo
of general merchandise for Fortune Is
land Sixteen days later, September 10,
the schooner ran into hurricane blow
ing with terrific violence from the north
east, veering around to the southeast
and continuing for three days.


Lashed by the gale and her decks swept
by tremendous seas, the schooner became
unmanageable. Her masts were whipped
out of her and her small boats were
smashed.


Crippled as she was the schooner rode
easier after her masts were gone ana
might have outlived the gale mad she not
sprung leak Heroic work at the
pumps availed nothing.


On the fourth day OF the hurricane the
captain decided to abandon his vessel
Fortunately tnere was slxteen-1oot
boat in tile vessels cargo. This was
equipped with provisions and water.


With great difficulty the eight men
managed to get away The gale had be-
gun to abate, but the sea was still run
ming high.


For four days and nights the little
craft was tossed about. On the third day
the water gave out.


The men had begun to suffer, when the
Seminole, bound south from New York,
hove in sight, took them on board and
carried them to Turks Island, where
they were landed and allowed TO remain
until the Seminole returned en- route to
New York.


The John A. Mathesen was built at
Essex in 1883 and was owned in Balti-
more.

CARLYLE, ILL.,, March 1.-Years ago
wild turkeys were abundant in the
dense timber lands of the state, espe-
cially in the bottoms of the Kaskaskia
river, and the expert hunter expert
enced no trouble in killing ALI he could
carry.


The birds were quite plentiful even
ten years ago, but a decided decrease
has been noted since. There are still
a few scattered flocks lin the timber,
and the true sportSmen assist the game
department in the protection of the
same, but the increase is not rapid.


The disappearance of the timber and
natural ranges for the big birds has
much to do with the shortage, yet
there is plenty of room for. breeding
and feeding places. This being the
case, several local sportsmen are going
to try an experiment. In a central
part of the timber there are several
wild turkey gobblers, and the intention
is to supply them with mates.


These turkey hens will be bought
from some farmer, taken to the tim
Der, and released near where the COB
blers range. Any person familiar with
the habits of the two varieties, the
wild and tame, know the tame ones
will readily get wild after associating
with the other variety. The project
ors of this propagating movement are
confident that the gobblers will soon
find the tame hens, which will result
in an increase of this rare bird. If it
is successful. several dozen turkeys,
both gobblers and hens, will be liber-
ated during the fall months.


Farmers living near timber land often
lose their turkeys because of their de-
sire to roam over the shaded bottom
lands. These incidents were of more
frequent occurrence many years ago.
since the wild ones would often entice
the tame ones away.

yacht Argonaut which left London

safety.

those on board barely had time to save
themselves. Fortunately the sea was
smooth and the transfer of the passen-
gers and crew to the small boats was
made speedily. There was no panic.
The people on board the Argonaut lost
everything they possessed.


For an hour the Argonaut's boats
groped about in the fog fer the
steamer Kingswell, which they finally
reached and boarded. Finding that
vessel in a sinking condition the pas
sengers again took to the boats and
were ultimately picked up by the
steamer Southwood, which brought
them in here.

NEW YORK March 2S.-The unusual
roughness of the sea during three days
of the voyage made the many passengers
of the Mauritania exceptionally eager to
land when the steamer arrived here to-
day. Two days after leaving Liverpool
the Mauretania encountered heavy
weather. and Monday night the waves
began to sweep the upper deck. which
is estimated about seven stories
above the water During the night
huge wave struck the navigation bridge,
breaking six of the heavy glass windows
in the courthouse. The officer duty
was cut about the face by the flying
splinters. All of Tuesday morning the
sea continued to be particularly rough.
and did not calm down till the following
day AS a result of the gale the Maure-
tania's speed was reduced to IA miles
during the worst day of the passage.

WEST POINT, n. Y, October 81
Princeton met the military academy ca
diets at foot ball here this afternoon for
the first time in two years. and the re-
suit was a O-to-O tie. Cold, crisp air
made the weather ideal for foot ball. and
both teams fought furiously, without
either securing decisive advantage.


In the first half honors were about
even, but in the second the visitors threat
ened to score repeatedly almost from the
time the whistle blew. Four times they
carried the ball to within the cadets
5-yard line only to lose 1t on downs.
Once they brought it to the 4-yard line
on a first down, but were unable to cross
the coveted goal line because of the ca
diets determined defense. Greble twice
saved the game for the cadets by tackling
Tibbott behind the line. while Johnson
and Brown also broke up several plays
at critical points.


West Point was dangerous only once,
in the first half. when by yeriesS of
rushes and fake kicks the ball was put
on Princeton's 4O-yard line. Dean then
tried to drop kick but the ball went wide.
In this half Princeton twice carried the
leather to their opponents 15-yard line,
but then West Points defense stiffened
and the visitors lost the ball.


Tibbott, Read and McCrohan were
Princeton's most effective ground-gainers,
while Greble and Kern alone were able
to advance the pigskin for the cadets.


A strong wind from the north handi-
capped West Point In the second half
and Princeton in the first. Neither side
took much advantage of the wind when
at their backs. punting being compare
lively infrequent.


There were many substitutions and one
injury. Dean, the cadets left halfback,
severely wrenched his knee and will be
out of the game for several weeks.


Despite the cold, high wind, the stands
were packed with spectators, and the
crowd was the most enthusiastic of the
season.

OAKLAND, Oct 24.=Pretty little
Vera Coy. 3 years old. was started alone
on this evenings Southern Pacific over
land train from Oakland pier for a long
journey to Kilburn, Wis. The baby
traveller arrived this afternoon from her
home on the Mount Hamilton road near
San Jose in charge of F.aW. Angler, the
Union Pacific agent at the Garden City
He had arranged for the journey and
had planned the details for the trip,
which should insure the safe arrival
of the youthful traveller at her destina-
ton


No little interest was taken at the
pier among the trainmen and passen-
gers in the plucky child who looked
forward to the long journey without
particle of misgiving. Angler explained
that his ward was being sent by the
mother unable to leave home, to Mrs.
Julius Baker, an aunt, in Wisconsin.
Miss Vera had been told that she must
go alone. and she accepted the situation
as calmly as though across continent
trips were weekly occurrences with
her.


Little Miss Coy was provided with
ample necessities and besides had been
carefully tagged, card being securely
fastened to her, which announced that
Miss Coy was travelling by Southern
Pacific, Union Pacific and Chicago and
Northwestern, consigned to Mrs. Julius
Baker at Kilburn, Wis. Her sleeping
car and berth numbers were also desig-
mated.


AS the train departed the little trav-
eler had already won her way into
the hearts of her fellow passengers.

figured in a remarkable animal story,
with a frog and snake in the leading
roles, and a diminqtive grandson
deeply wronged, holding up the heart
interest of the play.


On the Wax homestead, near New
port, there is situated a massive dwell

keep ajar the heavy front door there

frog, weighing four pounds and painted
green. This "amphibian" has been
worked overtime during this hot sum-
mer.


But Monday the frog was missing,
and diligent search was futile. Then
Mr.. Wax questioned his grandson. The
youth stoutly declared his innocence.

had thrown the frog into the we'll.

trounced.


thought the incident closed. But yes
terday James Bsline was blowing on
his farm, when he noticed a black
snake, seven feet long, summing him
self along the fence. Being a brave
man, Mr. Bisline killed the snake after

The unusual size of the reptile at
tracted his attention, and being in
quisitive, he made a post-mortem ex-
animation, which revealed the snake
had swallowed whole two half-grown
rabbits and the four-pound iron frog.

With their pretty faces filled with the
glow of health and their dark eyes re-
tecting the pleasant Impressions gained
in the Journey Of thousands of miles OF
ocean and land travel, two young women
from far off Australia the historic lahd
of the bush and the boomerang, and the
fleece and the gold, will leave Los An
geles this morning for Coronado after
weeks visit. during which time they have
thoroughly explored and filed their minds
with observations of the beauties of city
and surrounding country.


The travellers are Miss Nance Ryan of
Sydney Australia. and Miss Elsie steele
of Tasmania, and they, together with four
other attractive young ladies. are on a
trip around the world-education and
pleasure being their object


Dressed in natty costumes and with
the bearing of women able to take care
of themselves in any condition that might
arise, these young women as they travel
are objects of immediate interest because
of the strong personality which marks
them


Left Six Months Ago


The party left Australia six months ago.
and the first place at which their steamer
stopped was Suva, Samoa.


Every island was visited and the
pleasure gained was not unmixed with
instruction, for each member of the
party was filled with a desire for knowl-
edge and their Investigations were of the
most thorough character.


From the Samoan group the party
sailed to Sunbright island, whence the
cobra, from which large quantities of
soap is made, comes.


The stay there was short, and they de-
parted for Honolulu. Uncle Sans new
,n1n he on
greatly, and the stay which was planned
for this part of the world was extended,
while they made long trips into the in
terror of the islands, studying the ma
tives, industries and geography.


They landed on Canadian soil when
their ship touched the western hemi-
sphere, the first stop being at Victoria,
B. C. Thence they visited Portland. Sc
attle, San Francisco, San Bernardno.
At San Francisco the party was broken,
and while four of the girls returned
north for further study of conditions
Miss Ryan and Miss Steele proceeded
south.


Taking in the City


Los Angeles was reached a week age
and since their arrival the two young
women have visited all points of interest
in this vicinity.


The four women who went north from
San Francisco will arrive in Los Angeles
this morning, and the entire party will
then proceed to Coronado, from where
after few hours stay. they will jour.
ney eastward, the first stop thereafter t.
be made at Salt Lake.


A week or more will be spent in the
historic city of the Mormons, when the
party will leave for Chicago.


After a months tour of Eastern Can
ada the party will visit New York and
then go to England,


Egypt and the Orient will be the next
objective points of the trip, and it will
be some months hence when the young
women return to England and take the
steamer for their South Sea homes.


The young women are the daughters Of
wealthy sheepmen and miners of Aus.
tralia-men whose early life created ir
them a fearlessness and courage, health
and wholesome good will that has beer
inherited by their daughters.

national body acted the state had "A
right under it's ordinary police powers

an Irish giant. perhaps Finn McCoull
himself who built the Giants Cause
way, has been amusing himself for the
last few weeks by frightening the peo-
pie in the neighbOrhood OF Galway. One
Saturday night a couple of young men on

lage of Newcastle were crossing the rail-
way line near a place called Granville.
when they saw a human form about nine
feet high confronting them. When they
approached the specter it vanished, but
reappeared about forty yards further
down the railway, and was last seen go
ing in the direction of Tough Corrfb. The
young men brought the story into Galway
City, and the next night half a dozen of
their friends started to interview the
giants ghost. They were armed WITH
shOtguns and revolvers, and soon after
they arrived at the place they saw the
giant coming toward them One Of the
men raised revolver, but before he could
fire he became unconscious and fell into
the arms of his companions, who paid
no more attention to the ghost One OF
them declares. however, that he heard the
ghost laughing. The unconscious man
was carried into Galway, and taken TO
medical man. who revived him after
some hours work. Other parties went
out Monday and Tuesday nights, but the
ghost failed to appear.

NEW YORK, Jan. 5.-1ncipient rent
riots broke out on the east side today
as a result of the tension between the
landlords and the striking tenants, and
before the disorders were quelled by tho
police reserves, which were called from

injured and five were arrested.


The police used their clubs freely ou'
there was no way to obtain the number

The disorders were general throughout
the affected district. The most serious
trouble occurred on East Eleventh street.
where landlord who had been unable
to collect rent ordered his tenants to re-
move the Socialist flags which strikers
had used in decorations.


Police Use Clubs

holding mass meeting in the house. ana

Hardly had order been restored at this

r,ed to East Twelfth street, where strik-
ing tenants were making demonstrate
against a landlord who had objected to
the fiying of red flags over his property.
The crowd failed to obey the police order
to dispense and was set upon with clubs.


One woman, 1t is reported, was rem
dered insensible during the fight, in which
the wives and daughters as we'll as the
fathers and sons participated.


Strikers Bar Doors

the tenament, but the strikers barricaded
the door and a semblance of order hav-
ing been restored the officers withdrew.
Ambulances were summoned to care for
the injured, but the strikers declined to
admit physicians. stating that they would
call their own doctors.


There were several other outbreaks
which were checked by the police and
all during the day the teeming east side
swarmed into the streets and held i'm
promptu meetings. There were many
alterations between landlords and ten
ants and the reserves of four precincts
were kept in readiness to respond to
hurry calls.


Several mass meetings were held tonight
by the strikers. 1t was announced at the
headquarters of the strikers that the or
ganizing of the tenants in Brooklyn and
Jersey City was going on rapidly and by
February 1 over $1,000 tenants in the city
would be ready to enforce their demands
for lower rents.

stormy.

sight the American torpedo boat flo5
tilla, which accompanied the battle
ships from this port, but which turned
north at Smyth channel, thirty miles
from the western end of Magellan
strait, to proceed through this passage
to Telchahuano.

warships were spread out over a con-
siderable stretch, but all seemed to be
making splendid progress in the face
of the strong winds.

Heraldl In an editorial of the oath
you say existing conditions are

the threat of the Democratic party,
only made in the form that suits their
viewpoint? For many years the fight
has seemingly been Waged between the
two old parties and nothing has been
accomplished for the benefit of the
common people. Do you wonder the
people look for relief from another
source? The converts to Socialism are
coming in scores and hundreds from
both the Democratic and Republican
ranks-not soreheads, but honest, law

for the perpetuity of the government

err, you see the tidal wave approaching

overtaken, but fear not. Socialism
aims for pure democracy. The pres
ent Democratic wigwam is but tenn
porary, halfway house between Re-
publican plutocracy and pure, social

publican camp will make the through

not come to destroy but to fulfill. 1t

ually realizing it means the emancipa-

Newport, r. T., Sept. 26.-A etachment Of thirty
seamen gunners, equipped with diving outfits and
seventy naval apprentices from the Newport
pedo station went the stranded cruiser Yankee
Spindle Rock to-day, and the divers Immediately
set work patching up far as possible that por-
tion of her hull which was torn when the cruiser
aground Wednesday. The conditions of the
last week continued to-day, the fog being even
denser than before. making movements among the
eight vessels which alongside the Yankee dan
gerous.


The work of lightering the cargo of the cruiser
continued to-day. the great quantity of coal
which she carried being removed board the
naval golfers Nero and Lebanon.


Chief Constructor Washington l.. Capps and Con-
structor Grossbeck made to-day all the arrange
ments for salvage and supervised the construction
of the coferdam by which it is hoped 10 bring the
Yankee from her present dangerous position


naval officer who had just returned from the
stranded cruiser said to-day that the vessel was
held a Jagged rock about ten feet off her port
bow. Last night there heavy sea and the
Yankee pounded heavily, adding considerably to
the damage that has already been sustained. The
salving operations have necessitated a tightening
of the Yankee about the stern, and this has
disclosed that several frames have been
smashed.


The submarines which sailed for Cuttyhunk last
Sunday to participate in extensive man9uvres in
company with the Yankee have returned to Mar
ragansett Bay for further orders.


Chief Constructor Capps has called for
lighters from thesNewport coaling station be

FRESNO, Sept 6--John Bohanan, a
rancher living in the outskirts of the
Holland colony, shot and killed him
self yesterday morning, after fatally
woundiug his wife and shooting his
eldest son, Herbert, through the hand.


The shooting began over quarrel as
to the quantity and quality Of the
grapes growing on the Bohanan ranch
and the price the owners might expect
for them In all Bohanan fired nine
shots, four of which he directed at his
youngest son, Cecil, who fought desper-
ately to prevent his father from muir
dering his mother. The boy. escaped,
however, without injury.


It was shortly after o'clock yester-
day morning when the trouble between
Bohanan and his wife began. Accord
ing to the statement made to Sheriff
Chittenden after the killing the row
attracted little attention, as the Bo-
hanan family had been in the habit of
quarreling over every little thing that
came UP.


The husband and wife have not been
able to get. along well with each other
for years and the boys invariably sided
with their mother. This was the case
yesterday. Bohanan asserted that his
grapes were of the best quality and
QuduIllys the tdIEeSt IN quantity per
acre in the vicinity Of his home.


HRS. Bohanan dissented and from this
trivial cause the murder and suicide
came Mrs. Bohanan was removed to
the county hospital. She is not ex-
pected TO live At late hour last night
she was fast failing.


Herbert, the eldest son. will recover
from the wound IN his hand The In
quest win be held today on the body of
the suicide.

NEW WESTMINSTER, B. c., Dec.
1S--James jenkins and Jack Portella,
both negroes, and Lee Chung, a China
man, were hanged in the provincial jail
today.


Only when Hangman Radcliffe tight
ened the rope about Jenkins and
Chung's necks did they commence to
lose their nerve, but Portella never
moved a muscle.


They dropped together while Saliva
tion Army officers repeated prayers,
Sheriff Armstrong giving the signal
and Radcliffe pulling the bolt.


The three men stood on a single trap.


They slept well through the night,
Portella remaining in bed until the
guards aroused him to go to the gal
lows.


He smiled at the crowd of seventy
five spectators before the black cap
was pulled down over his face,


Jenkins assaulted and murdered
Mrs. Mary Morrison at Hazlemers;
Portella killed a mulatto woman in
Vancouver, while Chung killed another
Chinaman. Chung and Portella con-
fessed their guilt before the execution.
Jenkins did not.


The latter was convicted solely on
circumstantial evidence. and the chief
justice of British Columbia, who pre-
sided at the trial. interposed a stay of
sentence and ordered the case reviewed
by the full court, declaring the evil
dence was not conclusive; that there
was more than a reasonable doubt of
his guilt. He was overruled by the full
court.


AS soon as the Jail physician declared
the men dead they were buried in
graves already dug in the jail yard,
the bodies covered with quicklime and
the earth filed in by the convicts.

Little Holland, with Its 5,000,0 900 people
living safely behind their wave-washed
dikes, Is about to make new conquest
from it's old enemy, the ocean, writes
Emmett Campbell Hall in the Technical
World Magazine. Already Dutch en-
task which will result in turning the
Zuyder Zee into 1400 square miles of dry
land. Where of old the great Dutch
war fleets gathered where now 1000
fishermen sink their nets, there will rise
happy villages, broad pastures, popular
bordered roads and sleepy canals-new
farms and, homes for $4,000 Dutchmen.


The task to be undertaken is tre-
mendous one. 1t will cost nearly $780,
006 900. In return the government ex-
poets to secure annual rentals of more
than ST, 900 from those who occupy
and till the hard-won ground.


The Zuyder Zee has occupied a most
prominent place in Dutch history. On
It's shores are the ancient towns of
Medemblik. Hoorn. Harderwyck. Nor
den and Enkhuizen, under whose walls
the Dutch fleets used to lie at anchor
in the days when Holland disputed with
England the supremacy of the seas. 1t
seems peculiarly appropriate, now that
Holland has turned from the ways of
war to the paths of peace, that she
should win In great fight with the sea
"a fight that has continued throughout
hundreds of years--attaining victory
only by ceaseless vigilance and fierce
endeavor. And yet one cannot but ex-
perience feeling of regret that those
ancient cities which. though nations
rose and fell made good the circles of
their battered ramparts, defying alike
the power of the sea and the might of
Spain, should become quiet inland
towns, far removed from the roar of
the breakers against the dikes.

WASHINGTON. June 49, The

astronomers and spectators to the

with keen interest. The day could
hardly have been more favorable for
the purpose.


The first contact occurred thirty-five
minutes and twenty-eight seconds af-
ter o'clock this morning, which was
ten seconds ahead of the predicted
time while the second contact occurred
forty-nine minutes and two seconds
past noon, being twenty-three seconds
ahead of the predicted time.


The image of the sun was almost
perfect when the eclipse first occurred,
but it was not so good at the time of
the second contact, owing to clouds.
There were five scientists taking OBJ
servations with the different observa-
tory instruments, and the variations
of time among the different observers
was less than two seconds.


Prof. George H. Peters of the naval
observatory took seven photographs
with the photo-heiliograph, which
showed in addition to the moon pro-
jected upon the sun three fairly large
sun spot groups.

anchored. about three miles of the point,

mouth giving the latter's position and

Plymouth twenty miles east of the point.

and sent line aboard her preparatory
to towing her into Fall River The Massa-
chusetts, going from New York to Bos-
ton, was also standing by the Plymouth.
as was the New Haven, bound here with
freight. After five hours tossing about

was repaired and she went into Fall River
under her own steam.

Those who now advocating the substltu-

excellent argument for their case. According to
various competent witnesses the Chester police
made only perfunctory efforts to suppress the
rioters who warning against the local street
car company. but the state police quickly gained
control of the situation. The usual explanation
is doubtless correct; the local department had
too many friends among the rioters and could
not conquer the latter because it could not con-
quer its own human nature. Probably the
Chester situation is reproduced on a small scale
a hundred times every weekday in New York
City and several thousand times every Sunday,
when the honest buecoat soliloquizes: What's
the excise law between friends?"

Peter Palassou, a French milkman
| living ON his ranch in FELTON, street
near the San Bruno road, brought 80
years of stormy welded life to close
yesterday by killing his wife. A blood
| stained pitchfork, the crushed and bat
tered skull of his wife and the state
ments of his two children. who were
working in the loft of a barn at the
time, went to show that death was the
result of vicious and brutal attack,
prompted by q moments unreasoning
fury. The wife was 81 years old.
When arrested he shrieked out in
Mysteries that he had done nothing,
committed no crime; but when the first
flush of terror and flight had passed
he declared he had knocked her down
by slapping her face and that in fall
ing she had injured her head against
the stone steps of the barn.


DEED COMMITTED IN BARN
The deed was done In the barn of the
ranch shortly after o'clock yesterday
morning. The woman was helping her
husband spread the hay for the cattle
The two children, Auguste and Helen,
were In the loft above pitching down
hay to the father, who stood on plat


form with pitchfork in his hand. The
four worked in the silence of the work
ers OF the very early morn. In the dim


lantern light they could hardly see
themselves. The silence was broken


by the growing tones of the husband,


finding fault with the wife. The chill


dren looked at one another, shrugged


their shoulders and went on with their


work. 1t was an old story, this quar-


reling, this continual finding fault and
abuse. Then they heard their mother


reply In patient defense of herself.


The voices in the darkness below


ceased for an instant. Suddenly the


woman's shrek echoed through the


barn. They heard something smash


and body fall. The boy flew to his


mothers rescue and the girl followed
close on his heels. The father was


found standing by the mother, his
pitchfork on the ground, and the
mother lay unconscious the blood
flowing from her head, reddening the
hay.


ACCEPTED YEARS OF ABUSE


The blow struck yesterday was the
last Of many. For 80 years the woman
had accepted the abuse, the stormings
and beatings Of her master. Uncom-
planning, devoted, she remained by him.
From morn till night she worked for
him. 1t was she who MIXED the cattle
In the dim dawn; she cleared away the
remnants of the last meal. She had
worked away the beauty and spring of
her youth and then, gray haired, worn
and bowed, she tottered on working,
ever working. She saw her husband
gamble away the household money-I
and worked harder There were seven
children to care for, and she worked
still harder. And he took it all with
out thanks, without appreciation.
When gripped by sudden and insane
anger and his fists would go smashing
into ner racer she would crawl away |
TO weep in bitter loneliness. The time
came when even the well of her tears
was dried, but she worked on.


DROVE SON FROM HOME


She saw her husband drive her eldest
son from the home, and the bowed head
was bowed lower. She saw her daugh- !
ter Marie driven from the house by
ner husbands anger, and she accepted !
ms oictum. Then came more abuse, |
more beatings. And still she worked on. |


The two children, Auguste and Helen.
told the story yesterday. They spoke
In fiat. Unconditional voices, like chill |
dren whose lives had been one dull |
grind 1t was the story of a patient. |
awful martyrdom of s2 years, of a love
which passed all understanding.


on the morning of her death PaIassou
complained that she had left the door
OF the barn open. She said nothing and
worked on Then he passed the bounds |
and accused her of clandestineIy meet
ing other men. The gray head snapped |
back, and she answered him. Then
came the blow.


RECEIVERS CONSCIOUSNESS


The husband gazed on her as the how |
dashed water on the poor, old face and /
apparently satisfied, harnessed up his
horses and swung out of the ranch to |
deliver the mornings milk After ALI |
she was only unconscious and when he /
returned would be we'll as ever-at her
work. The woman recovered her CON
sciousness, threw her hand over her
eyes and staggered to her feet.


Her son helped her to the house. but
she never spoke q word. Her daughter
seeing the pain in her eyes, cried out
In alarm, but the mother paid no heed
Even death she took without COM |
plant. She went to her bed, Law down
and In a few hours died, without a
word. To the last she had held bv him


Palassou was taken to the central
police station. His children refused n
see him, but they went in mourning to
the morgue, where the mothers bodvI
lay, the anguish of her death lessenad
however, In the knowledge that her
work was done and her last blow re-
ceived. Then, weeping, they returned
to the home Of their desolation and
found the frightened cattle budding
away in one corner of the barn. away
from the patch of hay, dyed red with
their mothers blood.

hurled down the mountainside to the bottom of
a foot precipice was the experience through
which Nelson and Arthur Dale, sons Of G. Nell
son Dale. a Williams College professor. and a
young friend George Persist of Pittsfield passed
late last night. They landed in a tall henlock
tree which saved their lives. The horse was
killed and the wagon smashed into little pieces.


The three had started out Saturday for a two
weeks camping trip on Mount Greylock. Nell
son Dale the least injured. climbed down the
tree and summoned assistance, and the men
were carried to a nearby farmhouse.

part of the afternoon babies of all sizes
and kinds. in the charge of neatly
aproned nurses, gathered in the pretty
parlors where they were received by
the small host and hostess, Richard
and Katherine Grigg.


Mrs. Grigg has instituted the delight
full custom OF holding Juvenile recep-
ton each spring for the tiny sons and
daughters of the alumne of the Cum
mock school of expression. If the day
be fair the little ones frolic in the spa
cious garden, but when breezes from
the sea ruffe the red roses and over
cast the California sky with misty
clouds. the guests assemble indoors
and pass the afternoon in games and
other recreations familiar to the child
world.


Refreshments such as warm milk
and a bold array of animal crackers
add the final touch of enchantment to
the occasion and as the small guests
depart, dimpling with enjoyment, they
congratulate each other and them
selves upon the fact that they are
alumnae babies of Cumnock school.

PHILADELPHIA. August S.-Two per-
sons were killed and two others severely
injured by lightning during a severe cleo
trical storm that swept over eastern
Pennsylvania and New Jersey yesterday.
causing much havoc. Robert Heimbach,
a farmer, was struck and instantly killed
near Lewisburg. Pa. while working in
the fields, and Walter Cattell, aged seven
teen years, was struck and killed near
Glassboro. n. ]. His sister Mabel and
Rebecca Turner were also struck and Sc
verely injured, the latter being in a seri-
Gus condition. Cattell, his sister and
Miss Turner were seated under a shed
watching the lightning, when bolt
hit the peak of the house and ran down
a corner across the floor and through the
shed where they were sitting. The
lightning broke the legs off the chairs
and rendered the trio unconscious.


The charge passed down Cattelrs back
soaring the spine. and he was dead
when picked up. The shoes were
ripped from the feet of his sister. but
she recovered consciousness after short
time. Miss Turner remained half dazed
for some time and is seriously i'll from
shock One corner of Cattelrs home was
torn out by the lightning.


Buildings OF all sorts were struck in
various sections and destroyed and many
districts suffered from flooding. Philadel-
phia in connection with the storm, was
pelted by one of the most severe falls of
hail that has occurred in a number OF
years. Windows were broken. trees and
shrubbery beaten and torn and much
minor damage done. Half dozen rum
away accidents were reported to the po-
lice as a result of the storm.


The hailstOnes were as large as hazel
nuts, and when they came with terrific
force upon the backs of horses standing
in the streets the animals bottled, caus-
ing much trouble. The rain fell in tor
rents, and in all sections cellars and
streets were flooded.

orders to leave for the provinces, but

field near the barracks and defied their
officers.


The battalion from Salopika, which
ives drafted into the capital especially

to attack the rebels. They fired one
volley, after which the remaining
mutineers surrendered and were made
prisoners. Later they were drawn up
on the public square, tied together and
exhibited to the assembled troops as
rebels who had broken their military
oath.

PITTsBURG. Dec. 3.-Coal operat-
ors, mine owners, engineers. practical
miners, scientists and national and
state officials, all here for the meeting
of the mining congress, participated
this afternoon in the formal dedication
of the federal governemnts laboratory
and testing station established recently
in this city.


A series of tests in an artificial mine
in which conditions of real mines are
reproduced as far as possible, showing
the results from various explosives
and from so-called safety agencies, was
the most interesting feature of the
ceremony.


The first test was safety powder,
dry fire clay and bituminous coal dust,
the latter placed on shelves represent
ing lodges in mines. The powder was
fgnited for the blast and did not ex-
plode the dust.


There was a terrific explosion during
the fourth test, when IL pounds OF
black powder and twenty. pounds OF
road dust (actual mine dusD We're
used. The recoil was strong and the
flames covered the full length of the
artificial mine.


The test proved the combination to
be exceedingly dangerous. At this
point experts appeared bearing the
Draeger oxygen apparatus, including
metal and glass hoods, chemical cham
Der and air bag designed to render
breathing normal, or nearly so, while
the operator is surrounded by the most
deadly gases and vapors.


The men hurried into the gallery still
filed with fumes of the explosion and
apparently were not affected by any
of the gases. This device is designed
particularly for rescue work, and was
used with good results at Mariana.

Mabel Van Hazen was the prettest girl in
Westville, Conn, but there was not one OF the
troop of young people who spoke OF her with
envy, for she so unsefish and am1aDle no
one thought of begrudging her her position


How pretty she looked when the class of O5
fluttered across the Boardman High School plat
form! There wasn't lad in the graduating class
who did not feel willing to change places with
handsome Walter Horton when she smiled up
into his eyes every time some young essaylst
spoke of what the golden future might be. They
knew what it promised for although Mabel was
49, and three years older than the broad-shoul-
dered athlete they were betrothed lovers, and had
been for many day. Sixteen is not the age
when most boys begin serious love-making. But
Walter was a man of "a in appearance, and the
two had been sweethearts since they were chill
dren. They had grown up together in Westville,
pretty, quiet Westville, that hides in the shadow
of the granite hills, with never strange or
startling event to break the routine of the days.
Mabel sang in the Congregational choir and the
boy lover attended her everywhere, and both
families serenely waiting for the wedding
day that should cement their lifetime friendship.
Saturday Walter spent the evening at Mabels
home. But the lad was cross and the girl quick
tempered, and they quarreled. Sunday she could
not sing, and it whispered that Walter had
gone away. All the day Mabel laughed great
DEAL and the boys who called thought of Walters
absence with satisfaction. Then evening came,
and night, and she kissed her mother and father
and ran up to her little room.


"Thats a fine girl, mother" observed Mr.. Van
Hazen, proudly, and his wife smiled with moth
ers own gladness when she answered him.


Monday morning Mabel did not fill the rose
vases or show her fowerlike face in the break
fast room.


"Ill run up with cup of coffee for her." her
mother said. Then when she had been upstairs
a moment terrible cry echoed through the
house, and the father leaped up and ran wildly
toward it.


Mabel was lying with composed limbs and
serene looks on her little bed, but white powder
was on her lips and they found tnat she had
unlocked the gate of death with key called
poison.

Marjorie had a most beautiful doll, a
birthday gift from mamma. 1t was dress
ed in the very latest fashion, and the lit
tie girl sat by the hour in the big hotel
parlor holding her treasure in silent con-
tent Arabella was a wax doll with clear
rosy cheeks, and dark hair in curls like
Marjorie's own, and she now lay peace
fully sleeping in her new mammals arms,
the very loveliest thing Marjorie had ever
seen.


Presently the Queer Old Gentleman passed
blythe children always called him that
ever since the freezing night when he had
slept on the roof. When he saw Mar
iorie with the doll in her arms, he stop
ped for a moment in his walk and stood
in front of the fire, looking down upon
her.


What have you there, my childo" he
asked in mild voice.


Marjorie Immediately held up the doll.


Isn't she lovely?" she exclaimed.


The old gentleman took the doll in his
arms and examined it thoroughly. then
with a sudden movement lie laid it in the
heart of the glowing fire.


Such foolishness is not for sensible lit
tie girls" he said. Run outside, my
dear. and play with the dogs and cats
and chickens: some day you'll agree
with me-


But just now Marjorie didn't. for she
saw poor Arabella melting away before
her eyes. Shrek after shrek rent the
childish heart, and the Queer Old Gentle
man turned away with a shrug.


Then came mamma, and papa, and poor
little Marjorie was kissed and comforted
and went to sleep that night hugging a
new Arabella, and always after that she
kept away from the Queer Old Gentleman.

viewpoint of good football of a varie--

When the first half ended there had

line within seven minutes after play

Harvard had not scored, nor had she
been dangerous to the hitherto un"
crossed naval goal line. The crimson
score was made about the middle OF
the second half and was on a fiuke.
j. T. Doughty Nourse, from his place

There was drizzling rain that fell

goal posts. The navy punted almost

Harvard men knew what was happen

ward pass from Lange to Reiffsnider.

south of Montezuma in the authentic
report of the sale by Carlos Soto of
his Monte Cristo mine to parties well
known in Douglas who have asked
that their names be not yet given out.

their purchase known, but it is the
largest transaction reported in the
Montezuma district for many months.


The Monte Cristo mine is well known
i'm Douglas and Sonora among mining
men, and Carlos Soto is also well
known and extremely popular He has
operated the mine for several years
and has had several rich strikes in
that time, each time cleaning up a
tidy sum in shipments, but on every
occasion the strike pinched out.


Last September Soto made another
strike and from the extent of the vein
and the location and geological for
nation decided that he has at last
found the true vein and ore body. Min
ing engineers and experts agreed with
him, as did the experienced mining
men who have just purchased his hold
ings and intend to proceed with the
pushing of development and shipping
of ore from this rich silver proposition.

RUCHNER, in his Psychic Life of

trouble of working, attack well-stocked
hives in masses, kill the sentinels and

prises of this description they acquire

cruit whole companies, which get more
and more numerous; and finally they
form regular colonies of brgand bees.
But it is still more curious fact that
these brigand bees can be produced arti-
ficially by giving working bees mixture
of honey and brandy to drink. The bees
soon acquire taste for this beverage,
which has the same disastrous effect
upon them as upon men; they become
ill-disposed and irritable, and lose all
desire for work; and finally, when they
begin to feel hungry they attack and
plumber the well-suppiied hives.

ada. Artillery in solid mass headed the

western mounted police, the pride of Can

helmets, marching in platoons.

The storm. which gained in velocity

none fatally.

LONG BEACH, June 1.-THE drown
ing OF an entire family in the surf was
narrowly averted today by the prompt
and heroic action of Life Savers Noel
Ter and Cobb employed by the bath
house company. Probably 1900 people
standing awe-stricken along the pier
and the Pike witnessed the rescue ana
united in the cheer which went up as
the four endangered ones, father,
mother abd two daughters, were
snatched from a watery grave.


The man, w. f. Taylor, a travelling
salesman for the Toledo Scale COM
pany, and the girls were not In such
serious condition when rescued as was
Mrs. Taylor, who lay unconscious for
two hours while Manager Archer ana
attending physicians worked over her.
1t was feared for time she could not
be revived. This evening all four prac-
tically have recovered.


1t was shortly before noon when the
Taylors donned bathing suits at their
home. 539 Daisy avenue, and walked
down to the beach, The tide seemed
quite low and they waded out longer
distance than is usually possible. None
of the party could swim and they had
no intention of getting beyond a safe
point.


A sudden high breaker bore down
upon them, however, ana carrying tHeHh
off their feet whirled them about. AS
the wave ebbed they were carried along
by it. Taylor soon regained his feet
and in an instant had seized his young
est daughter Ruth, who was helpless
in the water close by. Mrs. Taylor and
the other daughter. May, he could not
see.


Moeller and Cobb, who were at the
life saving station on the beach repair
ing the life boat, had seen the perilous
situation and with great haste ran out
into the water, seized the heavy cata-
maran, which was afioat in the edge OF
the surf, and pushed it out to sea
Through the breaker line they sent the
catamaran with powerful strokes.
They saw the bodies of Mrs. Taylor
and the older daughter floating in on
the next wave and they lifted them on
the life saving craft.


Both mother and daughter were car
ried unconscious into the bath house
hospital Manager E. E. Archer. who
is frequently called upon to attend such
cases, knew just what steps to take at
once. and the little girl was soon out
of danger.

Leadville, Colo-A disastrous snow
slide occurred on Long and Derry hill,
near here, Sunday night, when about
800 tons of snow and rock swept down
the mountain side. The slide carried
away a part of the ore bins and shaft
house of the Aurora Mining Company,
in Iowa gulch, and came within few
feet of cabin in which half dozen
miners were sleeping. The men were
awakened by the roar and rushed from
their beds. They knew from the sound
that a slide was on its way down the
hill and started for safety. When the
slide had passed they saw that their
home had not been touched.

Cheyenne, Wyo.-The American car
in the New York-to-Paris endurance
race left Cheyenne at HIPS Monday
morning and reached Laramie, fifty
six miles west, at :45 p. m, making
the run over the summit of the Rock
les without mishap of any kind.


People were astir early to give the
racers hearty send-off, and long be-
fore the hour set for their departure
the streets were filled with enthusiastic
people. Shortly after 10 o'clock the
racer left the garage on Capitol ave
nue. and ran down to the Inter-Ocean
hotel, where E. Linn Mathewson, Har-
old Brinker, George Schuster, Captain
Hanson and others were photographed
in turn at the wheel of the big round
the-world auto. The moving picture
machine shot off several rolls of films
and at exactly 11:25, preceded by the
pilot cars and followed by number of
Denver, Cheyenne and Laramie autos
the start was made down West Six
teenth street toward the Rockies.


The trip over Sherman hill was
made via Granite canon, at which
place the route left the Union Pacific
tracks and entered Laramie via the
fish hatchery.


The weather is fine and the roads
are improving, and the American car
should make record time through Wy
oming. The racers appear to be in no
hurry, however


Mathewson will drive the car as far
as Ogden, where the wheel will be
taken by Harold Brinker, who will
take the car to San Francisco. From
that point George Shuster who has
been with the car from the start, will
be in charge and in all probability he
will take the car into Paris Captain
Hanson. the explorer, is still with the
car, and says he will be in the party
when the car reaches Paris.

of another man had not been substituted
for him, the corpse Of Dr. Henry B.
Cragin. formerly of Philadelphia, was
recently disinterred at Rose Hill ceme-
terry, this city. Until Miss Elizabeth
Burns of Chicago, whom the physician
was to marry. had closely scrutinized the
features. she would not give up a convic
ton that the man who had wooed and
won her was living.


In the physician's last illness neither
realized the seriousness of his affiiction.
Relatives took charge of the body soon
after the death. Before Miss Burns saw
the corpse ii was buried. The apparent
suddenness of the death and burial firmly
convinced her that the body was not
that of DIR. Cragin, but of another man
instead.


Parental objection to the impending
marriage was suggested as a cause for
the doctor being spirited away.


When Miss Burns finally. with the aid
of brother. who came here from New
York, saw the body and realized that
death had stolen her sweetheart. she
became hysterical. and is still in a
highly nervous state.

7HERE are but few Washingto-

not only founded their nation,

They still are here-those mansions of

Those who lived in them have gone to

From the time that John Smith, in 1908.

the hard headed old Scotchman conceded
the money that his property brought made

but in the laying out of the streets and

ing crane and singing kettle, and. while

mother country. The graceful aspens. the

In Finland everybody lives the SIM
pie life in summer. They camp out on
islands, in the forests. and always
somewhere near the water, for every
body swims and bathes.


Almost all classes sleep and eat al
fresco at this time of year, and the
town councils of the towns in this
progressive and altogether delightful
little country provide public fireplaces
and public bathing sheds in all places
where the working classes go in search

But the simple life is by no means
dull with the Firms. They combine it
with the surprising amount of gravity.
They eat, drink and are very merry

When they are tired of bathing and

watch fireworks and practice gymnas-

most healthy holiday makers in the

heads upon the branches, with their arms

ors with a persistence that made some

fleet.

NEW YORK, Aug. 3.--Miss Emily
Gardner, prima donna of the Abern
opera last year, was in the reception
hospital at Coney Island today suffer-

bulldog.


Miss Gardner's injuries and the shock
she suffered are serious and her con-
dition today was regarded as critical.


The bulldog belongs to Miss Gardners
housekeeper, who left the Gardner cot
tage last night after placing the dog
and number of puppies in the pantry


Miss Gardner entered the pantry,
whereupon the bulldog sprung upon
her, fastening his teeth in her left
arm.


The singer endeavored to fight off the
dog, but the animal tore at her arm,
decorating it terribly, snapped her right
hand, nearly biting off two fingers, and
bit her severely about the legs. Weak
with pain and terror, Miss Gardner fell
to the floor, but the dog continued its
attack upon her.


Meantime neighbors were attracted
by Miss Gardners screams, and the
dog was driven off. 1t is believed that
the animal is healthy.

search the captain and crew entered
cave In a rowboat. When the lights

boat. The ligths were extinguished

quest and yesterday the schooner

long I'm locating the food supply. and all

picking up the morsels as they rolled to

the sewer. Numerous fights took place.

meal that the ferry steamer Lackawanna
pounding her way through the ice less

to any extent.

CORRESPONDENT writing from Annapolis
near the close of the session said: 1.-THE DEM
ocrats reluctantly passed primary election
law for the whole State based upon the Balti-
more city law. Rural Democrats did not want
the bill because of the expense involved, and
they had to swallow it because Governor Croth-
ers declared that platform pledges are not
empty promises. There has been an interest
ing contest within the Democratic party over
the essential features of the bill, a contest in
which Governor Crothers and Senator Smith
have locked horns. Governor Crothers stood
for a popular primary vote, while Senator
Smith stood by the counties in their conten-
ton that the city would have too much pre-
ponderance in a popular vote. The Senator
has been the winner in the contest, and his
fight combined with his election, first to the
long term in the United States Senate, begin
ming March 4th, 1909, and his election to the
Senate to fill the vacancy caused by the death
of Senator Whyte, have easily made him the
Democratic leader of the State just as the gen.
eral course of legislation for Baltimore city
has made John J. Mahon the Democratic city
leader"

ST. PAUL. Sept S.-Judge vande-
renter in the United States circuit
court today granted the injunction re-
Quested by the st. Louis, Iron Mountain

operating in Arkansas, against the Ar
kansas state railway commission. The
injunction restrains the commission

Interstate traffic.

that the testimony IN the present hear
ing had demonstrated that the rates
proposed by the Arkansas railway
commission were unreasonable, nom
compensatory and unlawful and could
not be enforced against the railroad
companies.

ant give a bond, which will probably
be about 500, 900 each, that they would
keep a distinct and accurate account
showing the difference between the tar
Sn charges of the railroads and what
would have been charged if the rates
OF the Arkansas commission had been
applied.

-venter held that the law of congress
should take precedence over the law of
Arkansas in rate matters where the in
terstate rates impugned on interstate
regulations.

tail, following the swarms OF herring
and sardines, which have been plentiful

ing bait offered by the wharf anglers
late last evening. and were landed in
rapid succession until long after dark
It is the heaviest run of these fish since
last fall, when tons of them were piled
lpon the wharf in one day.

the Big Four railroad exploded today
while the train was running at full speed
badly injured. The train was wrecked
and burned. The concussion shook houses
and shattered windows for many miles.


Cars Blown Fifty Feet.


The freight train left Litchfield after
having been inspected by the crew, and
no hot boxes were reported. Two cars
filled with powder were in the middle
of the train. Ten minutes after leaving
here at sharp curve the two cars con-
tanning the powder were blown high into
the air and the whole train was wrecked.
Whole cars were blown fifty feet from the
track. and debris was scattered over
twenty acres of ground. None of the
train crew was hurt


The two men who were injured were
riding in a car some distance from the
middle of the train.


Whole Train Burned.

Tex, severely injured about the head, and
Paul s. Dougherty of Paxton, ILL.,, injured
internally. The letter carries an honor
able discharge from the United States
navy The injured were brought to st.

explosion was practically destroyed by
fire. Many cars consumed were loaded

miles to Greasy creek and there
hanged to tree.

from the direction of Adair and Rus
sell counties. They broke down the
Jail doors, dragged Hill out Che pro-
testing his innocence), placed him on
a horse and took him to Greasy creek,
where he was given a chance to pray
before being hanged.


No shots were fired, and no mutila-
tion of the body. offered. The mob
then quietly disappeared. The body
was cut down this morning.


After an assault Hill killed his
cousin, 13-year-old Mary Womack, in
Adair county, last week. Twice mobs
formed to lynch Hill, but were pre-
vented.


Last night no warning had been re-
ceived, and the mob worked without
real interference.

text:
Burglars blew open the safe in the
office of the Rosedale Transfer, Feed
and Fuel company, 1917 South Yer
mont avenue, early yesterday morning
and secured $50 in cash and several
checks amounting to $100.


Entrance was obtained by prying
open rear door. The men lost no time
in getting to work and did the job with
dispatch. They took every precaution
They poured nitroglycerin into the
crack around the outer door and into
the aperture made by knocking off the
combination dial; went into the feed
room and secured a number of sacks of
flour which they piled on top and
around the safe, set off the charge and
then gathered up the contents of the
safe and made their departure without
being disturbed or leaving any clew.


The explosion must have been ter
rife. The sacks of flour were torn to
the large outer door of the safe was
forced from it's hinges and lay on the
floor.


The robbery was discovered at 6
o'clock yesterday morning by Fleming
Franklin, senior member of the firm of
Franklin & Son, proprietors of the feed
yard, who stumbled over the wreckage
when he opened the office.


Two women living near by say they
heard whistling at about O'Clock, and
later heard muffled explosion.


The police were notified and are
working on the case. They say indica-
lions are that the job was done by
others than professionals, and think it
is the same gang that blew the safe
at the Aquarium bar, Eighth and Main
streets, Sunday night.

blocked the way.

head and started in. pushing the ice ahead and
70 the side. Six tugs were ranged along her

70 get her port side foot closer to the pier.

vanced again. The bow OF the vessel merely
skidded off from the ice mass. bringing the big
liner into exactly the same position she had
been in before.

VALPARAISO, Chile, February 15.-The
great American fleet of sixteen battle
ships, under the command of Rear Admit
raj Evans, passed Valparaiso yesterday
afternoon and continued on its voyage
northward for Callao, Peru. the next stop
ping place. All Valparaiso and thousands
Of persons from every city in Chile wit
messed the passing Of the fleet. President
Montt and the other high officials Of the
republic came out from shore to greet the
battleships. and almost the entire Chilean
navy exchanged salutes with them as they
swung around Curaumilla point and into
Valparaiso bay in single file. headed by
the Chilean cruiser Chacabuco and five
Chilean topedoboat destroyers.


Turning sharp around Curaumilla point
at 2:1O o'clock the Chacabuco and the
five Chilean destroyers led the Connecti-
cut and her fifteen sister ships into the
view of the thousands who had awaited
their appearance since dawn. The day
was perfect and the spectacle of the
fleet stretched in a great semicircie as
seen from the high hills around the bay
was magnificent.


President Was Present.


President Montt and other Chilean Of
ficials embarked on the training ship Gen.
eral Baquedano and took a position we'll
out in the harbor. Around the Baque-
dano the fleet swung at speed OF four
knots. firing the presidential salute as
they passed in review. 1t was one hour
from the time the head Of the fleet en-
tered the bay until tn last vessel had
passed the presidents ship and turned
toward the open sea. Then the Baque-
dano lifted anchor and escorted the fleet
he
north. 1t was a great review such as
had never before been seen in Valparaiso
bay. and the sight will long be remem-.
hered by the people of Chile who came to
witness it.


The shipping in the harbor ard the prin-
cipal buildings in the city were dressed
for the occasion. as the day was observed
as holiday in honor Of the fleet From
the picturesque. sloping hills. dotted with
houses. profusion of bunting and the
waving of flags was discernible from the
bay. Thousands of persons from Santiago
and other places in the republic had come
to Valparaiso for the occasion, and the
roofs of the Bolsa Commercial. with it's
two huge towers the custom house and
the large warehouses and other buildings
along the circular road skirting the bay
front were black with spectators.


Whole City Celebrated.


The enthusiasm Of the Chileans was al





as each battleship of the fleet swept
around the reviewing ship, their sides
lined with tackles in immaculate white.
and the bands playing patriotic airs. The
noise of the cheering was lost, however,
in that of the saluting guns from the fort
and the feet. Altogether. 300 shots
were fired


After the fleet had passed to the north
west a banquet was served on board the
General Baquedano by President Mont
Tn honor of the diplomatic corps and the
other guests. Toasts were drunk to
President Roosevelt and Admiral Evans
and his officers, crews and ships, and the
universal wish was expressed that the
Americans may have fair weather and
a safe passage to their destination.


In the city of Valparaiso at night cele-
brations of every kind were in progress.
and everywhere were heard words Of
praise for Admiral Evans for having hon.
ored Valparaiso with visit.

NEW YORK. September 10.-The most
decisive blow received by horsemen since
the anti-racing laws went into effect came
yesterday when it was officially announced
that the fall meeting of the Brighton
Beach Racing Association had been de-
clared Off William Engerman. treasurer
of the association. and president of the
Brighton track, declared that the meet
scheduled to be held from September y
to October would not be held. The fall
ing off of the attendance since betting was
prohibited at the tracks was the cause OF
the cancellations of the dates.


While horsemen anticipated q curtail-
ment of racing days at the Brighton
track. the announcement that the assocta-
ton had abandoned its entire meet came
like thunderbolt to them. and last night
the owners Of the track were vehemently
condemned. Horsemen cited the fact that
the association had made a great deal of
money year in and year out for many
years. and that they saw no reason why 1t
should close its gates fearing loss this
year.


The association suffered a loss during
its summer meeting and failed to pay
promptly some of its obligations. So long
did it withhold money from some turfmen
that many owners announced that they
would not race their horses this fall I'M
less prompt payment was guaranteed
them.


The abandonment of Brighton's meeting
was not the first indication that racing
was doomed in this state. Immediately
after Gov. Hughes won his fight against
the gambling interests the defeat of rae
ing was apparent First the admission
fee was reduced to s.. but the public did
not attend as 1t did during the days of
open betting. Then the Coney Island
Jockey Club announced that there would
be no racing at it's Sheepshead Bay track
on Fridays and the Westminster Associa-
ton followed with the statement that 1t
would hold only four days racing week
at Belmont Park.


Immediately after the anti-racing laws
went into effect Acting District Attorney
Elder of Kings began his crusade at the
Brighton track. After many bookmakers
had been arrested he procured indict-
ments against William Engeman. chief
stakeholder; Christopher Fitzgerald. the
president: John Boden. the secretary, and
John Cavanaugh. who was formerly in
charge Of the betting ring.

.Horsemen of the United States have
not often awaited the result of any ex-


pertinent with keener interest than
they are now following the efforts of


the department of agriculture to save
from extinction the vanishing type of
Morgan horse.


1t has been said that the old-time


Morgans, as a family, were nearer
perfection for all-around work in light
and heavy harness than any other


family of horses ever produced In this
country.


These horses were long and justly
celebrated for their admirable quail
ties. They were particularly remark
able for their great strength In proper


ton to their size and for their powers
of endurance. The Morgan horse,
though a small animal, was noted for


his bottom and hardness. as well as
for compactness and roundness of form.
He was a very sprightly animal and


was more sagacious than the general
ity of horses.


The Morgans of that day were rarely


more than fifteen hands high and were


even more COLBY and thick set than
the present day hackneys. Their heads
were fine and wonderfully expressive
of countenance, with small ears: necks


well formed, though rather short, chests


broad and deep, backs short, quarters
wide and powerful, legs short, fiat and
sinewy, with big bone and tendons. But
their most striking characteristic was
their carriage-stylish and proud In
the extreme, with quick, short trappy
action.


Popularity of the Morgans
| Fifty years ago there was no family
| of horses in America SO popular as the


Morgans. They were sought after In
every part of the country from Maine
| to California and Vermont, the place
of their origin, was well-nigh depopu-
| lated of stations to supply the breed
| ing studs of the west AMI south with
stock horses. This was before the


Hambletonians came into prominence
| through the fast performances of Dex-
| ter, George Wilkes and other trotters.
| When the craze for speed set in the
death knell of the Morgans was sound
| ed. Disregarding beauty. style and ac-
| ton the breeders went in for extreme
speed, and to produce 1t made reck-
| lessly general use In the stud of ami
| mails possessing no matter what de-
| fects of form, provided they were win
ners or came from winning families.
For racing purposes the Morgans were
| outclassed by the Hambletonians and
Mambrino Chiefs, and were soon sup
planted In popular favor by the fami-
| lies which gave to the trott1ng TURF


such celebrities as Dexter, Goldsmith


Maid and Lady Thorn. Breeders who


owned the best Morgans fastened to


cross them with racing stock. The


natural result was the alarmingly low


average excellence and the neglect and


finally the almost total extinction of


the 11organs.


| OF late years the high prices paid
| for carriage horses and the growing


scarcity of good ones have brought the


Morgan type again into high favor


among breeders. Many horsemen were
long ago impressed with the idea that
steps ought to be taken to revive and


perpetuate this valuable family of


horses, but there is question whether


the recent action of the government
authorities in this direction has not
come too late. First-class specimens
Of the breed are extremely scarce, even


in Vermont. This was strikingly DEM
onstrated a year or two ago, when an
| imported Arab horse at a leading YER


mont show won the prize offered for


the horse of the Morgan type.

COBB'S CREEK, CAL, Aug. 9.-This
has been a wonderful season for corns:
More and finer corns have been raised
here during the spring and summer
than for years past. All the known
varieties of corns have been raised,
from the tender green corn to the hard
yellow corn.


Almost any kind of shoe can be
utilized in raising corns, and 1t is a
regularity that a small shoe almost
invariably raises the largest corn. Local
experts are giving much attention to
this strange freak.


Unlike most crops, corns can be
raised by women as well as men and
without half the trouble. At the re-
cent grange exhibition Miss Sue
Howelis took the prize for the largest
and most perfect corn. Envious per
sons said it was not a corn and that
she should have made her entry in the
MON class.


Few persons are using moving ma
chine to cut their corns this summer.
some are employing saws, while the
more modern farmers, those who have
graduated from the state agricultural
college, show their training by using a
razor At the same time, the corn
knife has not been altogether discarded.

TIFLIS April 1S.-The situation on the


Persian frontier arising from the activity


Of bands of marauding kurds has not ma


terially improved. The Persian bandits.


who retired into their mountain Businesses


after their first successes against the


Russians, again concentrated in force yes


terday and renewed their attack against


Belesuvar.


The Russians countered with energy.


and their artillery bombarded several VIII


lagos in which the brigands had taken


shelter. The Russian commander has re-


ceived orders to disperse and entirely
wipe out the brigand bands. a reinforce
ment that went from Baku found its
tanks menaced by the brigands. 1t there
fore occupied points in Persian territory
in order adequately to protect the line of
communca ton.


Persians Mobilize.
In addition to the losses already report
ed the Russians have seven soldiers killed.
The Russian commander says in report
that the Persian authorities have lost
their heads entirely and that anarchy
reigns in the district.


Advices received here from Tabriz are


that the governor of that city has re-
ceived imperative orders from 'reheran to
hasten the dispatch of a Persian force
into the disturbed territory, sending all
the regular troops available.


Watching Turkey.
TIFLIS, April 1S.-Lieut. Gen. Mist


chenko, governor general of Tifis. has
left here for the Kars district to supervise
the precautionary measures Russia is TAX
ing along the Turkish frontier in view of


the mobilization of Turkish troops on the
other side of the line. The people of
Tiflis are considerably concerned over this
situation, but higher military officials now
profess confidence that the Turkish
measures are not directed against Russia.

ern part of Jewell county Thursday
night killed one man and injured
twenty-five persons, seven Of them
probably fatally. The storm travelled
from the southwest and was $50 yards
wide. 1t took everything in its path
and scattered a number of houses,
barns and small buildings over the
prairie. The property damage will
amount to thousands of dollars and
the damage to the growing crops is
large. The storm did considerable
property damage in Jewell, Cloud and
Clay counties, striking near Concor-
dia and Clay Center.

"Quincy Adams Sawyer" with a cast
of sixteen rural types" and two more
or less real people, reached the Grand
opera house yesterday afternoon from
somewhere up the line of the Southern
Pacific. At the Grand they were Joined
by the other members of the company
two sheep and white horse, with
buggy attached. The live stock and
accessories thereto lend atmosphere"
as it is called in stage technic, and
make the audience believe they are
witnessing the doings of real country
folk. The atmosphere" behaved them
selves much better than rural atmos-
phere usually does on the stage. The
only realistic feature lacking in the
play is a sheep-washing. The poor dear
sheepies sadly need their annual bath.


The rural types are the deacon and
his daughter, wife and houSekeeper, l.
farmer and his blind sister, a couple
of hired hands," ETC. The people"
are represented by Quincy Adams
Sawyer" a lawyer from Boston, and
his college chum, Arthur Hastings.
Hastings presence in the country is
not accounted for, but Quincy Adams
Sawyer went there for rest and recrea-
ton Hastings has annexed the affec-
tons of the village heiress, but her
foster mother will not consent to their
marriage. The love affair of these two,
which depends upon the clearing up
the mystery of the girls birth, is the
story of the play. There are several
other love episodes in the play, includ-
ing that of the lawyer and the blind
girl, but Indy Putnam and her fierce
old foster mother are the characters
upon whom the action depends.


Indy has been rescued from a
wrecked vessel and the only key to her
identity is a letter written by the man
who saved her, giving the name of her
mother. Lindy's foster brother falls
in love with her and wishes to marry
her. She will not marry him, and
when he dies, shortly before the date of
the play, he leaves her fortune that
seems immense to the rural community.
The death of her son and the fact that
his money went to Indy sets the moth
er's mind against her adopted dauGh-
ter, and she tries in every way to make
her life miserable. Among other re-
fined tortures, she hints that Linda's
parentage was not unstained. The
names of her parents she refuses to
divulge.


Enter the True Lover


Comes then Arthur Hastings and
gains her love. She elopes with him
and they are married.


The old woman in revenge declares
that the girl shall go to her grave with
out knowing her real name. IN tne
end, however, she relents and on her
deathbed tells Indy the truth.


This is the plot, but it is not the
play. There is the romance of Hulda
Mason and her rural lover, Zeke Pet
tengill, that was almost wrecked by the
mild Irritation of Hulda and Quincy
Adams Sawyer. Also there is the love
story of the man in the title role and
the blind girl, Alice Pettengill Hiram
Maxwell and Mandy Skinner are the
fourth pair of lovers and there are two
more of lesser Importance.


Besides the multiplicity of lovers,
there are the character parts of the
deacon and Professor Stroat. One is
the genial old farmer and the other the
local political boss. Both are excellent
as "types," though one who has not
had the privilege of residence at Ma
son CORNERS, Mass, cannot adjudicatee
their verisimilitude to the originals of
that peaceful vale.


Finally there are the foster mother,
Mrs. Eespibah Putnam. and her maid
of all work Samantha Green. If there
was nothing else in the play these
two would make it worth while. The
roles are handled by Annie Inman and
Clara Coleman and they should be the
highest paid members of the company,

FORT WORTH, Texas, April 1S.-i
With telephone. telegraph and railroad
service almost completely suspended
for two hours last night this is the
center of the worst wind and rain
storm that has ragged over North
Texas in many years.


With two exceptions every railroad
out of this city was forced to annul
some trains owing to washed out tracks
and loss of bridges, and at midnight
the telephone companies reported nav
ing lost all wires out of Fort Worth.


Clayburn, twenty miles south, was
struck by a windstorm' of tornado
proportions, followed by a torrential
downpour Of rain that literally flooded
the city. Within twenty minutes after
the storm broke the two bayous that
run through Clayburn had left their
banks, flooding five or six hundred
houses.


A circus whose tents were pitched in
the western portion of Clayburn was
completely wrecked. Two lions escaped
and prowled about town for an hour,
throwing the people into panic.


At Fort Worth the Trinity river be-
gan to rise again at midnight and
every available man from the police
force was hurried out to warn the peo-
pie living in the bottoms.


At least 5000 persons have been rem
dered homeless and ali streams are
still rising. Railroad service is badly
crippled. Five hundred delegates to
the state labor convention are weather.
bound here. A cloudburst in Parker
and Palo Pinto counties last night will
probably send the Brazos and Trinity
rivers two feet higher, and these
streams are now higher than in twen-
ty-five years.


Engineer Long and his fireman were
found dead under their engine today.
Their train left the track in a washout
d mile north Of Cleburne. Crops over
a large area have been destroyed and
the estimated loss will reach over half
a million dollars.
