An interesting incident of Christian mis-
sion work in Alaska is told as follows:


great feast was held by one of the
more southern H'lingit tribes. There had
been drinking and dancing and the men
and women were all drunk, for quanti-
ties Of the native ''hootsanoo' had been
furnished, and at last they lay upon the
floor in drunken stupor.


The little children were gathered out
side the house, tired and hungry. and
awfully afraid Of what their fathers and
mothers would do when they came to
themselves. for always after such scenes
there was fighting and blows and killings


One little girl eight years old named
Undah gathered the little group together
quietly and said: Come with me into
the forest and l will bring you food. We
shall have a feast, too So she picked
up little lame hungry baby that could
not walk and they all toddled after her
to the cedar grove outside of the village.
Then she told them that their fathers
and mothers were all ''hootsanoo dead"
and that they would be dead of empt-
ness before their mothers woke up un
less something was done. She was GO
ing to steal some food for them and she
wanted some of the older ones to help
her. but she would not let any one help
who had ever stolen anything before for
themselves They all kept very still and
several of the brightest boys and girls
slipped out of the group aud came and
81 God beside her. Then she spoke To them
in a lower tone and told them there WAS
something else for them to do besides
steal food. They must first find all the
knives and guns and weapons of every
kind in the village and hide them SO that
when the elders woke UP there would be
no killing. So she left the children In the
forest to wait for the food and took her
little company of helpers back to the vii
lage From house to house they went
gathering up knives and guns and any
thing that could kill. They put them In
Undah's blanket and she took them all
and MD them beneath a hollow log I'm the
woods. Then she went to her uncle
storehouSe-he was also the chief and her
master and guardian-and unlocking the
door spread out her blanket and put in
it dried berry cakes and punches of sea-
weed, bundles of dried salmon ana the
little candle fish. She folded the blanket
together and gave 1t to her assistants to
carry to the children. Then taking
horn spoon. she filled two wooden dishes
with berries and fish eggs preserved In
oil. which she carried and fed to the
younger children. Then she organized
some more helpers TO play games WIN
the children all the afternoon. and until
early evening when the smoke from the
village chimneys showed that the parents
were waking up and getting supper, and
they might safely steal back without no
tice. But great was the wonder when il
was discovered that every ones knife and
gun were gone! They thought the witches
had done it. But in the night little Undah
stole out fearfully. for they all believe
there are eri! spirits abroad at night and
brought the weapons and laid them in
conspicuous heap In the village street.
where they were found with wonder and
awe the next morning by their owners
This feast was notable among all the
tribes because not single instance of
serious quarreiins occurred, and 50 no
injuries had 10 be avenged or paid for
~ few months later Undah heard of the
mission school and begged SO long and so
sweetly to be sent that she finally was
allowed to go. She became A Christian
was bright scholar and finally married
Christian young man who had been
trained a carpenter in the Industrial
Training School at Sitka. and is doing a
great work among the natives Just by
showing them what sweet, beautiful
Christian home can be.

NEW BRITAIN, Conn.,, July 26.-To
all appearances Mrs. William McNulty
was dead for one hour on Saturday aft
ternoon. This is admitted even by her
physician, DR.. Thomas Mulligan, a
hard -headed, Unconditional person who
seeks only scientific facts. He says
hers was remarkable case of sus-
pended animation; the more remark
able because while her body seemed to
have become but a shell of clay, her
mind was active.


"Oh, [ have been far away" she
sighed, when speech was restored to
her. Do not be afraid to die; l have
never experienced such a blessed SEN
sation.


Psychologists, spirituallsts, those who
seek to raise the veil from what has
been the unknowable, can study these
facts:


Mrs. McNulty, about 60 years old, 10
as estimable as unimaginatiVe; she
loves her family and her home. Her
friends and neighbors esteem her
highly. She has been ill. While seated
In chair Saturday afternoon sne Pc
came unconscious; her family, IN
tensely alarmed, hurried messenger
for DR.. Mulligan, who has been treating
her.


Seemingly She Had Died


On examination the physician found
that she had ceased to breathe. He
detected faint pulse at her wrist but,
quickly, that disappeared; her heart
had stopped beating; seemingly she
was dead. Her mourning family began
to arrange for the funeral.


But Dr. Mulligan was not perfectly
convinced that he had lost his patient.
He sent for his electric battery and APP
piled a very strong current to the APP
parently lifelesS woman.


Seventy minutes had passed since she
lost consciousness, when the muscles
of her neck twitched slightly. DR.. Null
ligan continued to apply the current;
in five minutes more Mrs. McNulty
made a deep inhalation, then breathed
family, but regularly; then she re-
gained consciousness.


Saw Friends Long Dead


Mrs. McNulty was asked where she
had been and whom she had seen. She
answered quite nationally that she had
seen many people, some old, some
Young, and among them her mother
and a relative who had been dead for
thirty years. She said she spoke to
them and was intensely delighted with
the conversation.


She was asked if her journey had
been pleasant, and she answered that
ii had, and in describing the place
where she had been she said 1T was
beautifully illuminated, not by the sun,
moon or stars, but by a most peculiar
light, remarkable for it's beauty and
brilliancy

Washington Oct. I-The Interstate Commerce
Commission has decided that regulations made by
railroads governing Communication tickets must not
discriminate between classes of persons. as has
been done frequently by carriers which offer special
inducements to school children.


Complaint made some time ago that certain
railroads allowed school children TO ride their
trains at reduced fares. while they compelled work
ing children to pay the regular rate The commits
sion holds that this regulation is unjusty discrlrli-
natcry and unlawful. Railroads are permitted
however to use communication tickets limited in
their sale to children and young persons between
certain ages. Such an arrangement will provide
the desired rates for school children and will not
exclude other children travelling under substan-
tally similar circumstances. 1t is also calculated
10 protect against the Of such tickets by
adults. The new rule forbids ticket agents from
inquiring into the business of the passenger as a
condition for fixing the transportation rate.

Quebec July 24-The Prince of Wales has had
another day of strenuous activity, beginning
this morning with grand review of the troops,
sailors and marines on the Plains of Abraham,
then officiating as the title deeds of this his
toric battlefield were turned over as a perma-
nent memorial. between times attending gala
luncheons and dinners and finally tonight min
Cling with the gay throngs OF beautifully
dressed women at the state ball at the Parlia-
ment buildings The prince is bearing his part
in these functions with all the dignity and good
nature of his royal father, shifting his uniforms
from admiral TO field marshal and then TO plain
and we'll groomed English gentleman. and al
ways awakening the enthusiastic cheers OF the
crowd whenever he appears.


The grand review of the military and naval
forces was the spectacular feature of the day.
The forces assembled the plains far ex-
ceeded the armies of Wolfe and Montcaln,
which fought for mastery of the same grounds.
the aggregate to-day numbering twenty-three
thousand, while the spectators raised the as
semblage to nearly fifty thousand. A vast hol-
low square inclosed the reviewing grounds, slop-
ing up from the cove where Wolfe's men gained
the heights and wrested the field from the
French.


Spread out over this plain were the troops
and bluejackets, glfttering assemblage of red
coats grenadiers, Highlanders and the mounted
COWBOY forces Of the Northwest. The five hun
dred American sailors and marines from the
New Hampshire showed to good advantage,
their steady marching winning full share of
cheers. The prince rode on the field wearing
the brilliant scarlet uniform of a field marshal.
the helmet topped with red and white plumes
and his breast crossed with the blue sash of the
Order of the Garter. He galloped along the
long extended front. the regimental colors
tro0 rolling hUglas
sounding the royal salute as he rode along.
Beside MIN rode Field Marshal Lord Roberts,
or "Bobs." the soldiers know him. sharing
the welcome given the prince


After inspecting the men the prince and Lord
Roberts took positions before the reviewing
stand, while the columns def1led past for
than an hour. Vice President Fairbanks and
his military staff occupied seats on the review
ing stand. and joined in the cheers which greet
ed the American contingent as it passed the
prince. The American sailors wore yellow leg
gings and natty white duck hats which con-
trasted with the straw hats of the British tars
and tr,e topknot caps of the French sailors.
The review was the most extensive in
this country, and one OF the largest in time Of
peace ever held in America.


Following the review, the prince formally
transferred the battlefield to the Governor Gen.
erai a lasting public memorial. Heretofore
1t has been owned in parcels by private parties,
but the princes dedication to-day passes it
over to the government.


The state ball at the Parliament Building
tonight is the chief social function in course
Of the princes stay. The building was brilliant
ly Illuminated within and without and great
throng filed the Senate chamber, which tenn
porarily served the purpose of a ballroom.


The American officers gave a dance this af-
ternoon board the New Hampshire, which
was largely attended by officials and women.

holds the long distance sending record

The Matson navigation company's
steamer Hilonian, Captain Peter John
son, which arrived late Wednesday
night from Honolulu, had a good ex-
cuse for being more than 80 hours late.
If the Hilonian had not been a stout
ship, well found and in good hands,
steamer, passengers and crew would
probably be at the bottom of the
ocean, for the storm through which
the steamer passed was one of the
worst that the oldest sai1orman aboard
had ever seen. 1t did to the Hilonian
more damage than the II inch shells
did the next day to the monitor
Florida.


Head winds were encountered all the
way from Honolulu, but 1T was not un-
til Tuesday morning that the north
west wind developed hurricane force
and things began to happen on the
Hilonian.


The wind gave preliminary exhi-
bftion of it's strength by converting the
deck awning into ribbons and tearing
the weather cloths from along the rail-
AS the wind increased in fury SO did
the waves gain in size, and by after
noon green seas were playing tag over
the liners bridge. The steel pipe COW
ers were torn away like so much
paper and at 5 o'clock it seemed as If
the whole Pacific ocean was trying to
climb aboard. Suddenly the sea lifted
the skylights from their fastenings and
water poured below, flooding all the
staterooms and converting the saloon
into a natatorium.


One passenger, Mrs. True of Oak
land, was so terrified by the noise of
the bombardment of water against her
stateroom that she tainted and was
carried with great difficulty TO the sa-
loon.


All the passengers spent Tuesday
night huddled together In the saloon,
while on the bridge Captain Johnson
and his officers fought the storm. So
violently did the seas assail the ship
that the officers were afraid that the
matches would be broken open. But
the Hilonian weathered the storm. All
hands were turned to Wednesday with
buckets and mops drying out the flood
ed staterooms and everybody enjoyed
some rest the last night at sea- The

proposed franchise changes of the Los
Angeles railway are accommodating. The
Third Street Improvement association
met this afternoon and took action, the
purpose of which is to defeat the rail
road company's intent to remove its
tracks from Third street.


The chamber of commerce of Venice,
which has protested against good roads
and free postal delivery in Ocean Park,
Is now also protesting against the rail-
roads running time schedule. Action
along this line was taken last night and
will go in simultaneously with the pro-
testing action of Santa Monica bodies.
Manager Sherman of the Los Angeles
Pacific has already promised certain
improvements.

A BOUT December the forty odd United
States revenue cutters begin their winter
cruise along the coasts. The term revenue
cutter gives an inadequate notion of the varied
duties of this most efficient service.


Revenue cutters are the hfesavers of the
seas. They patrol the coast regular beats,
looking for vessels in distress. They suppress
mutinies, smuggling. and illicit seal hunting.
examine ships papers, enforce quarantine regu-
lations supply lighthouses, and are in general
the police department, fire department, am
bulance corps, and messenger boys OF the sea


The service was formed at the instance of
Alexander Hamilton. during his administra-
ton of the Treasury Department. In 1901 ten
cutters were built and put in commission under
rules that Hamilton wrote. In time OF peace
the cutters are under the Treasury Depart
ment; but when breaks out they sub
ject to the authority OF the Navy Department.
From the War of 1917 to the Spanish American
War they have always done good work.


1t Is IN time OF peace that the cutters tight
their hardest battles. Every year they save
many lives and average OF three million
dollars worth Of property.

its best endeavOrs to prevent the rescuers
from pulling the would-be suicide from
the water. Henry P. Turpin. aged ABOUT
thirty-two years succeeded in drowning
himself I'm the old Pennsylvania canal at
Steelton. near here.


Turpin spent the night drinking and
early in the morning accompanied by his
bull terrier went to the canal and plunged
headlong into the stream. which is very
deep at that place Edward McCord and
Frank Magnolia saw Turpin in the water
and made an attempt to reach him, but
the dog sprang at them. biting piece of
flesh from the wrist of Magnolia. The
dog was thrown aside and held by an
other man, while McCord and Magnolia
swan to the side of Turpin and dragged
him ashore Turpin appeared very angry,
because the men would not permit him
to commit suicide.


Third Attempt Successful.


Shortly after 6 o'clock he returned to
the canal and again jumped in. Another
attempt to reach the man was made by
the two men. but the dog attacked each
one and bit McCord on the neck. Once
more Turpin was rescued and the men
telephoned for a policeman.


Before he arrived, however, Turpin. with
the assistance of his faithful dog. got
away from his rescuers and made a third
and successful attempt to end his life
Turpin ran to the canal. yelling good
bye and jumped in. Once more the men
followed. but, the dog more vicious than
ever, chased one after the other from
the edge of the water. One of the men
successful in passing the dog and jumped
into the stream, but the dog followed and
attac ed him.


After spending some minutes trying to
pass the dog and get into the stream, an
officer arrived. and by shooting at the
animal, scared him from the canal. The
rescuers then succeeded in dragging Tur-
pin to shore after considerable time spent
diving for the body. but the man was
dead.


Turpin was the son of James P. Turpin,
who committed suicide ten years ago.

To the Editor OF The Star:


The demand for gathering and plant
ing forest tree seeds is from two
sources: first. from the hundreds of
thousands Of square miles of denuded
forest lands of the northeast and south
east United States for reforesting.


The other and more pressing neces-
sity is from the thirteen great timber
less plains and prairie states and ter
ritcr!es west of the Mississippi river.


About four months ago the superin-
tendent OF trees and parkfngs here very
kindly gave me permission to gather
tree seeds from the street trees of this
city. which number about 95,0U0--the
greatest number and variety of any city
tendent of the Capitol building and
grounds extended similar courtesy to me.
And since September ,, while gathering
forty EIGHT sacks of forest tree seeds.
approximately two millions of good
germinative quality, twenty-three sacks
of which / have planted in Virginia,
about two miles west Of Falls Church,
have been thinking of the stupendous
work of supplying the two demands
from the sources mentioned and of Il
simple method of accomplishing this
great work of reforesting and forest
ing the east and west, namely, by gath
ering and planting the tens of millions
of forest tree seeds that are annually
produced ana wasted IN TINS city an
nuaily.


The children. under efficient direction.
could gather and plant many millions of

d. c.. every year. The forest tree seeds

ers. The Norway maple is a superior

stems hold the leaves in nearly a hori
zontal position.

S. A. GAYLOR.

ing the building. For nearly twenty
minutes the battle continued. Then
the Devil, by deft flank movement,
sank his fangs into Nigger's throat and
a minute later she fell dead.

The one hundred and twenty-five odd miles along the New

greatest pleasuring section in the United States.


Upon the bluffs Of the northern end and the gently shelving
sands Of the southern end are located forty resorts which enter

seekers.


At no time in the year is this section more delightful than
during the spring and early summer months. One who has not
seen them at this season would marvel at their delights. The
great pine belt, which extends through the center Of New Jersey,
fills the air with ~lie-gving ozone, which, combined with the salty
tang Of the sea and the open air exercise possible at all times, is
exhiarating and tonic to the highest degree.


Long Branch, with its beautiful cottage -neighbors, West End.
Hollywood, and Elberon; Deal and Allenhurst, largely devoted TO
cottage life; Asbury Park and Ocean Grove, attracting thousands
yearly; Avon, Bemar, Como, Spring Lake and Sea Grit, are a
galaxy Of attractive places upon the bluffs where "the country
meets the sea-"


Then the Banegat Bay section, where Point Pleasant, Sea
Side Park, Island Heights, Banegat City and Beach Haven,
with other smaller places nearby, welcome the summer ojOurner.


Atlantic City, with It's seven miles Of beach and drives, and
its charming suburbs, leads the island resorts, separated from
the main land by the great salt marshes.


Ocean City, Sea Isle City, Avalon and Stone Harbor; Anglesea,
Wildwood, Holly Beach and Wildwood Crest also have q large
summer population.


And Cape May, with its new million dollar hotel and its won
deriul improvements, makes a fitting climax and holds a high place

The Pennsylvania Railroad is the direct route to all OF these
resorts from all sections Of the country. Its splendid train service

NEW YORK, June 1.-Whirling up
Ocean Parkway. Brooklyn. at a speed Of
fifty miles an hour early today. a big
touring automobile containing a party OF
merrymakers who had spent the night
at Coney Island crashed into a tree.
bounded into the air. turned turtle and
fell upon the occupants. Two men were
instantly killed. and two were so severely
crushed that they may die. Two other
men who were in the car escaped almost
without a scratch.


The dead are:


William p Goubeaud.


Thomas Nolan.


The injured:


Victor Brandes. right arm and left thigh
broken and internal injuries.


James Mckenna. left shoulder broken
and possible internal injuries.


All four lived in Brooklyn


Man at the Wheel Arrested.


The automobile was owned and driven
by John Lanyon Of Brooklyn. In the
automobile with Lanyon besides the two
men who were killed and the two injured
was Ernest Eggert.


Lanyon. who was at the wheel of the
machine when the accident occurred, was
arrested.


The accident Is believed to have resulted
from q disarrangement of the steering
gear The car was flying up Ocean Park
way at tremendous speed. but apparently
under perfect control. when 1t struck the
curve. When Lanyon turned the wheel to
bring the car around 1t responded easily
and promptly at first but then with
sudden swerve 1t darted toward the curb
and crashed against a tree. Goubeaud
and Nolan were instantly killed when the
heavy car fell upon them. and Brandes
and Mckenna were so severely crushed
that they were unconscious when they
were removed from the wreckage. Lanyon
and Eggert were stunned, but quickly re-
covered.

MANILA, July 27.-A destructive
typhoon swept over Hongkong at
midnight last night, causing heavy loss
OF life among the Chinese residents
and unroofng many buildings.


The tyrhoon caused tempestuous
seas which resulted in several steam
ers being driven ashore.

the offices of the Pacific Mail Steam
ship company and the Kingsclere hotel
The former building collapsed COM
pletely. while portions of the hotel
crumbled to the earth from the force
of the hurricane.


There was no loss of life reported
among the foreign inha bitants.


The British steamers Persia and
Schuylkill and the coasting steamers
Charles Hardouin and Lai Sang were
battered against the shores, where at
last reports they were still resting.


The crew of the British cruiser
Astrae performed gallantly in attempt
ing to rescue the Chinese crew of a
derelict junk After battling desper-
ately in the mountainous seas for over
an hour the Britishers succeeded in
rescuing six out of total of thirteen.
The remaining seven were drowned.


The property loss on shore will be
heavy.

The romance of Charles B. Woodbury.
and Olive Lorsue, a romance that began
years ago, that prospered. and then fell
into evil days, came to an abrupt END

When the two met years ago, Wood
ward forty years old, the girl only
eighteen, it was a case OF love at first
sight, and their friends believed that
no match could have been more happily
made.


And for a time after the marriage
several years ago romance did live with
them and life went smoothly enough.
in spite of their varying ages and their
different views of life.


Finally the time came when the strain
was 200 great, the whole fabric fell.
and for two years not word was
spoken between them


Then IN February, 1904, came Sepa-
ration, and for the long period Of nearly
three years they went along the bust
ness of living, each striving 10 forget
the existence of the other.


Ten months ago Woodward filed a
petition for divorce, alleging incompati-
bility and making other allegations.
Yesterday Justice Gould made the de-
cree, and the romance of forty and
eighteen ended.

but try as hard as he might there were
only two words he could say. One was
Him. m M H-m-m- -mp' and the other

In the morning as soon as the boy

was welcome. Sometimes Tony would
rub his nose gently on the boys sleeve

little pony would listen with both ears
and sometimes say quietly, Him. H-m
H-m." just in sympathy


One night when all the family were

house caught fire.


Tony, who was. not asleep, had very

danger that was at hand. so he kicked
down his stall bar and pushed open the
sliding door with his nose and ran
swiftly round the house, crying
Neigh. N-e-i-g-hl'' at the top of his
voice.


The boy walked up and called the rest

After that the little pony did not
wish to learn any new words. for he
knew that two given him were the very
best and most useful ones he could
have.

freight train were carried down and the
span was totally demolished.


William Wilson of Havre de Grace,
a watchman, went down with the
wreckage and received injuries which
may prove fatal.


There were no other casualties.


The bridge, which was erected in the
early eighties, was being rebuilt and
double tracked. The accident occurred
about o'clock. With crash that was
heard for a distance of several miles,
the immense mass fell into the river,
completely choking up the eastern
channel.


Two hours later the section that went
down would have been swarming with
workmen engaged in putting up the
great steel beams and girders which
enter into it's construction.


There are reports current that the
bridge was tampered with. and that
dynamite had been concealed in differ
ent parts of the structure during the
past few weeks.


Baltimore & Ohio officials are on the
scene making Investigations.

WASHINGTON, April 1.-Two hun
dred residents of California and Ore
gon, who have been summoned to
Washington as witnesses in the Hyde
Benson land fraud cases, about 20 per
cent of whom are women. are prao-
tically stranded in Washington.


The howl that they are sending up
reverberates through the corridors of
the courthouse, and the indignation OF
the westerners that their congressman
did not look out for them when the
urgent deficiency bill was put through
has made more than one member OF
congress shake in his political shoes.


The principals in the now famous
land fraud case are at liberty. although
under $4,000 bonds. The Jurors have
been taken from their occupations and
families probably for four months, and
the witnesses, called from their homes
in the far west. are stranded in a
strange city.


Every day many of the witnesses go
to the office of the United States mar
shall at the city hall and draw the
SIPS, which must last them till the
next day, when they repeat the opera
ton. The protest of these witnesses
is very loud.


The deputy marshals have been
driven almost distracted by the appeals
of the witnesses, but are powerless to
aid them.

OAKLAND, July 10.-Regardless of
consequences TO herself, Miss Julia
Leonard of $50 Mead avenue smothered
with her hands and with q sheet hastily
caught up the flames which enveloped
the body of her year old niece, Celia
McBrerty today. Though her right
hand was badly scorched and though
she risked her own clothing catching
fire, Miss Leonard's heroic efforts were
unavailing and the little one died at
the receiving hospital in. agony four
hours after being taken there.


Little Celia, a bright faced child with
brown hair and eyes, procured matches
from an unknown source and went to
play alone in the back yard. No one
saw her set her dress ahre and her
screams gave the hrsr intimation Of the
accident.


I was sweeping" said Miss Leonard,
when I heard Celia screaming and I
ran TO the back door. She was running 3
around in the yard with her clothing
all ablaze. I snatched a sheet from
the clothes line and smothered the fire
as soon as 1 could get 10 her. Then 1
tore of the burnt clothing, wrapped
her in the sheet and as soon as the po-
lice came 1 brought her TO the hospital
in my arms"


The child's mother has been dead for
Two ears. Out neE ulDLleE COulQ not
have bestowed more loving care upon
her than did Miss Leonard today. The
little girl screamed for her aunt as she
lay on the operating table, and only
when the woman's lips were pressed
against the blistered flesh of the baby
face were the cries stilled for an in
slant.


"Auntie, auntie, don't go away. Take
ne home again" she walled, while the
surgeons and attendants worked,
swiftly wrapping the child's body in
long bandages saturated with soothing
oils. The burns extended from the
right knee upward, enveloping the
front of the body and part of the back
on the right side. The chubby face
and neck had not escaped the flames
And the curly brown hair was badly
burned above the forehead. Death oc-
Cured at 3 o'clock in the afternoon.


Only when the work of caring for
Celia had been finished and the opiates
had induced sleep did Miss Leonard
realize her own condition. She sank
into a chair with her head on the op-
Grating table, moaning and saying that
she wished she had been the victim in
place of the child. DR.. W. H. Irwin
dressed her hand and wrist and ad-
ministered restOratives when she COL
Iapsed.


The little girl was the daughter Of
Daniel McBrerty. a hOd carrier.

wreck

scoped. Engineer Nichols had received

most quiet spot to do her work When

commotion possible.


The warmer it gets the quieter she

cret. She hangs a wet sheet. not drip
ping wet, across a line in her room.

good idea,

At the dawn of day on July 3. 1868,

face to face on the plains of Gettys-
burg. This day was causing much
anxiety to many people both in the
north and the south. A little skirmish-
ing took place before the real battle
began. and the scouts were gathering
information about the opposing army's
position. The union troops were the
first TO charge. and led by their brave
leader, charged upon the confederate
works, but were driven back with
heavy loss. Time after time they
would charge. and with the same re-
suit. Many boys in blue" fell under
the murderous fire of the confederates,
but all the time the rebel line was
weakening under the enemy's fire and
was crumbling to pieces in the center

great charge and their superior num-
bers told on the rebels decreasing
troops, and they swept on, on, and
on. until the confederates fed in mad
retreat across the plain. The tri-
umphant army followed and many
thousands fell in the pursuit.


Soldiers who had fought on this bat
tie ground have proudly erected monu-
ments to show where they stood.


AS evening gathered the moon burst
out in full light upon an awful scene.
dead men being scattered for miles
around. and the meanings of the
wounded broke upon ones ear as the
poor men suffered. Thus ended this
battle.

paying expenses.

laborers bound to their Guatemalan
employers for three years.


Ignorant of the language and in a
land where the law is sometimes the
dictator's will, it was easy to keep
them on the plantations, where they
slaved until their plight was made
known to the British government. This,
however, was not until eighteen years
had passed and most of the natives
had died. Those returning have little
to show for their years of toll.


Capt. Blackburn was lost at sea In
December, 1894, when the Monserrat
went down with all hands.

Inclosed by dark gray fog, cold
and impenetrable. eight boys spent
Monday night adrift in an open boat
beyond the heads, reaching safety only
yesterday morning when the incoming
tide swept them ashore at Angel island.
In the darkness of the mist the youths
feared that they had drifted to some
far off land, but with the breaking of
the low lying clouds and the arrival of
assistance they learned how near they
We're to home. All through the night
anxious parents waited for news of
the missing lads, who had gone for
pleasure sail but had failed to take
warning from the descending vapor.


The boys who participated in the
eventful cruise were: George Land
ridge, years of age, of 1912 Green
street; Wilfred BaIk. Is years of age,
of 1853 Vallejo street; Thomas Costello,
% years old, of 1927 Webster street;
Lee cambridge, 10 years of age; George
Opperman, 19, who lives in Scott street
near Filbert; Frank Suffers, @15,- of 3047
Van Ness avenue; Joseph Cul1iane, I9,
of 1929 Larkin street, and Joseph Ri
ordan, % years of age.


The boys live in the vicinity of the
Dolphin boat club at the foot of Van
Ness avenue, and. own in partnership a
boat which they keep in the waters
there. Monday afternoon George Land
ridge. Wilfred Balk and Thomas Co.'S
tello took short sail in fiat bottomed
boat and, returning in the evening met
the five other lads and a night sail
was proposed.


OVERTAKEN BY FOG


At s o'clock in the evening the eight
boys set out in what they called the
rock cod boat. 1t is we'll ballasted and
has made trips on the open sea. The
youths sailed out to the center of, the
bay and were enjoying their cruise
without observing the lowering mist
Gradually the wind died down and they
found themselves becalmed. The fog
gathered quickly and in a few moments
their vision was obscured by the dark
gray curtains. They had lost their
sense of direction. They strained their
eyes for the flash of the lighthouse,
but stared only, into the grayness For
a long time they were silent, as the
realization came that they were help
less.


The occasional splash of the sea
against the side of the -boat told them
that they were drifting. They tried
to row, but their efforts only took
them further into the mist They then
sat silent in the boat and listened
After half an hour they heard in the
invisible distance the warning sound of
the fog bells. AS they drifted the bells
rang clearer and clearer and then they
knew they were being carried beyond
the bay through the heads and out into
the open sea. The tide was running
full through the gate and they were
swept toward the Farallones. They
took turns at the oars but the intense
cold made a mockery of their strokes.
Two of the boys were without coats
and the mist, which had become driz-
-zle, drenched their clothing.


OARS ARE USELESS


Then came seasickness. The swells
at the bar rocked the craft and all
save Costello were overtaken by ILL
ness. In. a desperate endeavor to re-
gain the bay the boys tugged at the
oars, but after an hours exertion could
see no evidence of land.


All through the night and the hours
of early morning they struggled wildly
at the oars, stopping occasionally in the
endeavor to get their bearings. But
the fog had only thickened. Suddenly
the boat crashed against a rock. split
and the boys were thrown upon the
shore.


They pulled shattered parts of their
boat on land and started fire. not
knowing whittier they had driftea.
After some hours two of the bows
started on a tour of exploration. They
encountered two soldiers and learned
that they had landed on Angel island
From there they were brought to the
city by the island tug, and quickly
communicated with their homes.

SAN RAFAEL. Dec. 22.-Unconscious

from leaking gas jet, T. c. Evans, for
many years member of Pinkerton's
detective force at San Francisco and
now town detective for San Rafael,
was rescued from his bedroom In the
Shafer house this morning. After work
ing two hours over the unconscious man
Dr. Galehouse succeeded in resusci-
tating him and he is now out of dan
ger. Owing to the cold weather Evans
closed all the windows OF his rooms be-
fore retiring for the night. In turning
off the light he did not completely shut
off the flow of the gas. Toward morn
ing one of the other roomers noticing
the odor. traced it to Evans apartment.
Repeated knockings at the door did not
rouse the man and finally the lock was
forced and the detective taken from the
poisoned atmosphere.

Lawrence O'Brien, an Illinois Central
engineer, risked his life in cab filled
with scalding steam yesterday to save
his train from wreck.


When the southbound mail and eX-
press was nearing the city a patch on
the boiler gave way. The cab was filled
with steam, while the hot water poured
out in a stream. O'Brien and Fireman
Thomas Slick plunged through the open
front windows of the cab and took
refuge on the running board. Crawling
back through the narrow opening,
O,Brien groped in the suffocatins
steam, found the throttle and closed 1t
and applied the brakes. Until the train
stopped with jar the passengers were
unaware that anything had happened.


O'Brien was slightly scalded.

LOS ANGELES, June 25.-[Editor
Herald: The death of Mr.. Cleveland
leaves the country without living ex-
president. This has happened three
times in our history. The first was
from the death of Washington, in 1899,
to March 4, at noon, 1901. The second
was from the death of Andrew Johnson,
January 25, 1875, to March 4, at noon,
1877. The death of Cleveland will leave
the country without a surviving ex-
president until March next, at noon.


The president who lived longest after
his term expired was John Adams. He
survived twenty-five years and four
months to day The next longest sur
yiyor was John Quincy Adams, who
died twenty-five years and eight
months after his presidential term ex-
pired. Martin Van Buren and Millard
Fillmore lived little more than twen-
ty-one years; James Madison, nineteen
years and four months; Thomas JEFF
ferson, seventeen years and four
months, and John Tyler about fifteen
years. None of the other ex-presidents
survived above twelve years, Cleveland,
Pierce and Hayes reaching near that
period.


The earlier presidents survi d longer
than the later, though as rule they
retired from Office more advanced in
wears. 1t is a peculiar fact that three
presidents whose terms were IN sue
session died on the Fourth of July.
They were John Adams, Thomas JEFF
ferson and James Madison.

LITTLE ROCK, Ark. November "a
Reports regarding the destruction by yes
terday's tornado are still indefinite. but
indicate no change as to the number OF
fatalities. which has been conservativeiy
estimated at thirty. The lose Of property
will 60 into the hundreds Of thousands
Miles upon miles OF land have been swept
bare. Forests, homes. business houses
and churches have been demolished in
many communities. Several dispatches
say that whole forests of trees were
torn out by their roots and that many
buildings that were not demolished were
lifted from their foundations and twisted.


Thus far reports differ as to the gen
eral direction of the tornado at the Diff
ferent points. Two reports from Berry
vile. where homes were destroyed and
three people injured. were to the effect
that the tornado came from the north,
while another report said it came from
the west.


Two Tornadoes in Duel.


From all reports there appears to have
been different tornadoes. one starting from
the south and the other from the north.
both dipping to the earth at Intervals
and apparently meeting in the central
western part of the state. where the most
damage has been reported


The town of Pfney. a German settle
ment on the Iron Mountain railroad be-
tween Knoxville and London, suffered the
most. The number of dead is variously
estimated from nine to twenty. Five
business houses and several homes were
DESTROYED. according to reports.


All the physicians of Knoxville have left
that place for Piney, travelling in buggies
and automobiles. Nothing has been
heard from them.


From the towns Of Berryville and
Cravens the most definite reports are re-
ceived. At the former place three per-
sons were injured and the property loss is
roughly estimated at between $4,000 and
$4,000.


At Cravens four persons are known 10
be dead. members of the family of John
Rosin. farmer. who were caught under
the falling timbers Of their home. L. q.
Holt and wife. an aged couple were seri-
ously injured and may die.


Injured and Missing.


Eight persons who took refuge in a
store were caught in the crash of the
building and all were injured. Eight
others are reported as missing.


At Cravens nearly all the larger build
ings were either demolished or badly
damaged.


A dispatch received from Knoxville
early today partially confirms the report
that the village of Barr. four miles from
that place. was totally wrecked. Section
men who went to the scene state that the
entire intermediate country has been laid
waste by the wind and hail which fol-
lowed. the hail in some places standing 10
a depth of six inches.


In the vicinity of Mulberry five persons
are reported killed and others injured.
AT Lodi one woman was seriously injured
and the Methodist Church and several
other buildings were destroyed.

NEW YORK, July 15.-The new era of
electricity on the New York. New Haven
and Hartford railroad ended suddenly for
about two hours yesterday afternoon.
soon after the thunderstorm reached the
city, and as suddenly came back to its
own for a brief space. that snorting,
smoking iron steed, the locomotive.


Commuters on the New Haven had
been praying for a thunderstorm to
break the long spell of heat. They were
flocking into the Grand Central station
at 4:3O o'clock yesterday afternoon when
out Of the clouds came a lightning bolt
which effectually put the roads electric
system out of business


AS far as the electricians Of the COM
pany could figure last night. this bolt
landed on the overhead wire at Wood
lawn. Wherever It did land the current
failed. Every train on the New haven
from Woodlawn to Stamford. Conn.
stopped. Between Woodlawn and New
York the system was all right. Trains
could move In and out, but from Wood
lawn to Stamford the overhead wires
were useless and the blockade was COM
plete.


Meantime the New York Central trains.
which are run over separate tracks, suf-
fered no delay at all.


When New York was informed that the
electrical system Of the New Haven had
failed, w. G. Baird, the general superin-
tendent got busy trying to locate the
cause of the trouble. But the trouble
could not be remedied all at once. While
the electrical experts were busy the trains
were piling up. SO hurry call went in
for the long discarded locomotives. There
was no way Of breaking the blockade and
getting the tracks clear except by the use
of coal and steam.


The roads nearest big reserve of loco
motives. was in the big roundhouse at
Stamford. Conn. There the locomotives
pick up the trains after they have passed
the electric zone. They also provide for
the freight trains that plod along from

BERLIN, March 3O.-The emperor and
empress have made elaborate arrange
ments for their stay in Castle Achiileion,
Corfu, where they will soon arrive from
Venice They have taken with them a
large suite. comprising a court marshal.
two aides-de-camp, six officers OF the
guards, two physicians, twelve body serv-
ants and secretary for the emperor. and
a court marshal two ladies of the cham
Der, two equerries and six domestics for
the empress.


The culinary possibilities of Corfu are
not being relied on, no fewer than
twenty-four cooks and maids are going
from the castle to attend to the imperial
kitchen. Even kitchen utensils from the
Berlin palace are to be forwarded thither.


Two imperial carriages and six touring
automobiles are under way and also two
transport motor cars for the baggage.
Ten chauffeurs, with eight helpers. are to
look after these machines.


Horses, too, are to be shipped to Corfu.
and twenty grooms and coachmen will go
with them.


The Castle Achilleion, which lies nearly
1000 feet above the sea level. has been
connected with the lower surrounding
country by a small cable elevator. Post
and telegraph offices have been erected,
SO as to keep the emperor in constant
communication with the outer word,
while the roads in the island, usually of
the most primitive description, have been
vastly improved for the occasion.

Der canyon, nine miles from Santa
Paula. Two oilmen, who had been
drilling wells on the mountainside be-
low where the bodies were found, made
the discovery. There was no snow
near the bodies when found, but there
was evidence in plenty in the drifts
about that snow laid thick all about.


The boys must have met death some
time Thursday. 1t is supposed that
they got lost on some of the winding
trails and wandered about until they
sat down to rest. The bodies were
taken to Santa Paula late tonight.

In spite of the complaint of John H. o'Brien.
Commissioner OF Water Supply, Gas and Elec-
tricity, that the New York Central & Hudson
River Railroad acted without authority in build
Ing its overhead tension system of electricity be-
tween Hishbridge and the city line the Public Ser
vice Commission has dismissed the complaint
After many hearings and careful inspection of
the system by Commissioner Eustis, he has de-
cided that if would be a great injustice TO the
company 10 compel 1t to expend S,5oooO or 5000
600 in replacing fits present system with under
ground system. especially when both the experts
for the company and for the city have agreed that
the system is practically safe be made
and that the railroad has shown willingness to
make any changes that would improve its safety


The company had its line entirely completed
when Commissioner O'Brien made the complaint
last March that the permit issued by his prede-
gave it right to erect overhead high
tension system. During the hearings on the matter
the citys electrical experts testified that the Cen
trails system was the safest kind of overhead con-
struction, and counsel for the city admitted that
whenever any suggestions to its improvement
had been made by the city authorities the road
had brought its system TO the highest state of
perfection to which overhead construction be
brought


Experts for the company disagreed with those
for the city that underground construction was
safer than overhead, and the evidence showed that
the company had experienced more serious trouble
from its underground than from its overhead lines.


Commissioner Eustis in his Investigations was
impressed by the fact that though the city was
making efforts TO compel the Central to place its
wires underground. the Long Island Railroad on
the other hand. under permits from the city, had
erected and maintained forty miles of overhead
high tension wires within the city limits The
commissioner failed to find evidence that these per-
mits were temporary, asserted by the counsel
for the CITY, Furthermore, a comparison of the
two systems showed that the Central had used
much greater precautions in fencing OFF it's right
of way than had the Long Island. He also found
that in the various boroughs there were more than
five hundred and fifty miles of overhead wires used
for trolley or electric light service that. were far
more dangerous than the wires of the Central


The commissioner distinctly states that he does
not express preference for the aerial system but
is acting the evidence submitted in the In
question. The commission also adopted his recon-
mendation that the request for the removal of the
high tension lines to the easterly side Of the right
of way he Harlem division. north of Wood
lawn Road be dismissed Commissioner Eustis
finds their present location is the safer one.

railroad discovered what had been done
last night they sent for tugs and tried
to shift the Edmund Butler out of the
fairway to allow their boats to reach
the float. but SO far all efforts were I'M
availing.

less search for the big British collier
Silberhorn, which is now supposed to
have been lost with all on board In the
South Pacific ocean, somewhere near
San Fernandez island (Crusoe's island),


off the coast of Northern Chile.


The Silberhorn was loaded with coal,
which she took on at Cardiff and was
to discharge at Guayaquil. She was
reported several weeks ago as having
been sighted near Fernandez island,
on fire, and the gunboat went out from
Valparaiso, on her way north, with or
ders to look for the collier. She cruised
about the islands for some time and
examined several of them, but without
getting trace of the missing vessel.
The Shearwater will remain here until
Tuesday and will then sail for San
Francisco, where she will take coal for
the continued trip to Esquimaulr. The
summer will be passed in Boring sea.
and meanwhile the gunboat Algerine
will take her place in southern waters.

The actual work of the day was

turrets fronting a rather shabby Sec

hued summer gowns and with hutter-
ing fans and waving handkerchiefs.
Higher up another gallery topped the
vast enclosure.


High up above the vast assemblage

steel girders looped with bunting and
ablaze with electric devices, while on
every side the national colors were
woven into sunbursts, shields and pa
triotic symbols.

Just back of the Ohio leaders werc

1t was truly a gathering of the giants

ator Burrows of Michigan. The vener-

NEW YORK, December 12-With only
bloody finger prints of the murderer to
assist them. the police today are securing
the city for some trace of the man who
committed now what appears to be one of
the most battling crimes in the city's
criminal history.


His victim, the young woman whose
body was found last night in padlocked
and barricaded apartment at 337 East
18th street, has not yet been identified
A thorough search of the rooms has re-
yealed nothing which will aid the police
in their task.


Every distinguishing mark had been re-
moved from the woman's clothing. Pic
lures had been cut from their frames and
burned. together with several pieces of
paper which may have borne addresses.


On every hand there was to be found
evidences of the crafty care used by the
murderer to battle pursuit.


The discovery of the crime came about
through the anxiety of the janitress OF
the flathouse to collect rent for the
apartment, nearly two weeks overdue.


The man and woman who occupied the
rooms more than two months had paid
promptly up to the first of the present
month. Since that time the apartment
hal been closed, the door locked with
paddock on the outside. and neither the
man nor the woman had been seen.


Last night the janitress decided to enter
the apartment to make sure the tenants
had not removed their trunks without
her knowledge The police were called
to assist her in opening the padlocked
door.


When an entrance was forced the wom-
ans body. with head almost severed.
was lying on the blood-soaked bed. The
room was in confusion. Broken chairs
were scattered about and wearing apparel
which had been removed from an open
trunk was strewn about the room.


Under the womans body lay razor,
It's edge hacked and broken. The con-
ditior of the body indicated that the wom-
an had been dead not less than two
weeks On the dOorknOb and on the
sheets were the finger prints of the MUIR
derer.

NEW YORK, June 17.-Searchlights
played over the lower bay last night
from Forts Wadsworth and Hamilton,
while national guardsmen and regu-
lars engaged in the defense of New
York, against mimic enemy, ready
at the first news from Sandy Hook to
man the batteries OF huge guns and
blow the invading fleet out of the
water as soon as it got within range.


Infantrymen at the same time pa
trolled the outpost to protect the forts
from attacks in the rear, which were
expected about the time the battle with
the fleets began.


After evening parade the guards
were doubled at both forts and actual
military conditions prevailed. None
save the men in uniform could gain
admission to either encampment with
out passes. The searchlights were
flashing over the narrows from both
forts and every craft between forts
and Sandy Hook was brought out into
clear relief. The men behind the
searchlights were taking no chances of
being surprised by the enemy for lack
of illumination.


All night the lights flashed over the
bay and the soldiers, both professional
and amateur, slept lightly, ready to
jump their places at the first alarm
But the night passed quietly and day.
light came without the enemy" hav-
ing put in an appearance.


1t is almost certain now that the at
tack will be made.


Later: Tugs In Battle


The tugs representing the hostile
fleet attacking New York approached
Forts Totten and Schuyler in Long
Island sound tonight. The search
lights had no sooner revealed their
presence that the call to arms was
sounded. Immediately twelve and ten
inch guns of the batteries began to
boom.


After half an hours bombardment the
hypothetical battleship was pronounced
out of action. Twenty minutes later
two more hypothetical battleships were
theoretically sunk, and four hypotheti-
cal armored cruisers were declared to
have been put out of action. The
"warships" then withdrew. Several at
tempts to land hypothetical troops were
repulsed by the national guardsmen.

following the four yachts which left

Honolulu. In describing the trip he
said:


I'VE left San Pedro with the racing
yachts After rounding the second
stake, the Lurline was leading, with
Gwendolyn II second, Lady Maud third
and the Hawaii fourth. The Lady
Maud was being handled very nicely
and was giving the Hawaii the leach

"At o'clock they were in the same
order, with about half a mile between
each of the first three and the Ha-
wall about two and one-half miles
astern. At 4:30 o'clock the Gwendolyn
passed the Lurline and a little later
the Lady Maud did the same. At 1880
o'clock all four yachts practically were
becalmed within hailing distance of
each other, the Hawaii having come
up with a late puff, which held her
longer than the others.


I'VE left them in this condition and
went over to Avalon, about twelve
miles, and anchored at about p. m.
we leIL Avalon DIT Os0U U CLOCK OunUdy
morning and headed for the easterly
end of Clemente island, expecting to
find the racing yachts ten or fifteen
miles beyond Clemente. Instead, how
ever, we picked up the Lady Maud
and then the Lurline about 1880
o'clock, about fifteen miles this side
of Clemente. They had not made more
than eighteen or twenty miles during
the night. The Gwendolyn also was
in sight. The Hawaii could not be seen.


Captain Johnson of the Gwendolyn
said the last they had seen of her was
about IL o'clock Saturday night and
she then was about five miles astern.
We visited the three boats and took
their mail, which consisted of twenty
one letters. All the men were de-

though they had been out two weeks

sweethearts.


I'VE stayed with the three yachts

made a circle to southwark and found
the Hawaii about o'clock some TWEEN
ty miles astern the other boats, which
at that time were just clearing Gle
mente with light breeze The men on
the Hawaii reported that they had been
becalmed all night and that the tide |
had carried her out of her course. She |
had Just begun to catch the light breeze |
when we found her. The other boats |
had caught it two or three hours pre-
viously and indications were that she |
would get clear of the island by Sun
day night We collected four letters

Of the leaders. At 1880 o'clock Sunday

weather prevented any fast sailing"

overturned. Nevertheless, the coaches
sent them through long signal practice.

freshmen.

tim. Five tugs were busy for more

The British Yeoman, which arrived

of coal was hove short about 9 o'clock
yesterday preparatory to being towed
to the China basin wharf to discharge
cargo. Before the tug arrived the Brit
ish Yeoman's anchor, almost on the
ground, began to drag and before Cap
tain Peter Hilton realized that any
thing was wrong his ship was moving
of the Drummuir. Chain was paid

afterward carried away, tore big
hole in the bulwarks on the Yeoman' 3
starboard quarter. ripped the mizzen
rigging adrift, smashed two sets of
iron davits ard did considerable dam
age about the Yeoman's decks.


The Drummuir's forerigging was car
ried away and the huke OF the Drum
muir's port anchor was jammsd into
her port bow. making a ragged hole.
fortunately above the water line.


The tugs Relief. Fearless, Restless.
Sea Queen and Sea Lark were hastened
to the scene and by noon the British
Yeoman was anchored at a safe dis
tance from the Drummuir and under
writer's surveyors were taking count
of the damage on both ships.

w. S. Waterston of Invercargill. n. D.,

Waycross. Ga. June 27.-Walter Wilkins and

brought here day from Wayne County, one
charged with outraging the fourteen year old
daughter of Wiley Wainwright on Thursday
evening. They were being taken by Wayne
County officers from the Jail there to Jesup for
safe keeping, when the mob rushed the officers
and hung the two prisoners.


In the rush dozen hands clasped each officer
and his gun. The negroes were jerked across
the railroad track and Il hundred persons
pounced upon them, others still holding the
guards. Through the wire fence of the rail-
road the mob showed the negroes. and then
started on a run across College Hill. For

oak tree in the old Cherokee Nursery. Here an
attempt made to break the handouts which

was broken apart and a loop was made

chain tying 1t around the limb, while others
held the negro up from the ground. He was
then turned loose his feet about two feet from
the ground. The other negro. still handcuffed
to the body of the hanging man, stood with
hands clasped around the tree. The mob, step
ping back about ten PAGES. opened fire upon
the men, hundreds of shots being fired into the
bodies

who was casping the tree. there being doubt

could be done to stop the enraged mob, how

NEW YORK, September 9-Berthe
Claiche, the French girl who in July.
1905. was driven to kill her white slave
master. was yesterday granted her free
dom by order of the parole board. which
had found that since her Incarceration in
the state prison for women at Auburn
she had never violated single rule of
that institution.


Where she is going the authorities de-
clfned to say. The girl had begged that
her destination be kept a secret.


She says she has reformed and that she
IS eager TO live in a community where she
Is utterly unknown. She declared she
did not want to see New York and the
Great White Way again


Berthe Claiche had been brought to this
country by Emile Gendron. who used to
send her out in the streets at night and
then make her give him her earnings.
When she did not bring money enough to
please him he beat her


Finally the girl went to the Tender
loin police station and complained. Two
detectives were assigned to arrest Gen
dron. The girl said she would point him
out Gendron happened along and was
placed under arrest. He and his captor
walked ahead. while Berthe and another
sleuth followed


They had gone only short distance
when the girl suddenly drew a revolver
from her waist and fired two shots at
Gendron. killing him She was arrested
and indicted for murder


In June, 1906. she was permitted to plead
guilty to manslaughter and sentenced I'M
der the indeterminate sentence system to
the state prison for women at Auburn
On account of her excellent behavior she
has earned a full communication


When she first went to Auburn she
spoke but little English. In prison she
has attended school. and has become quite
proficient in the English language. She
also joined the church there


When the girl was told yesterday that
she had been granted her freedom on
parole she broke down and wept hys-
terically.

San Francisco.-Eight thousand blue
jackets and marines-the largest
armed force the American navy has

war-were landed Thursday from the

ever known.

of their shipmate bands and to cheers
that began with the first command to
march and ended only when the sailor
men had again embarked in the small
boats that returned them to the bat
tleships and armored cruisers in the
roadstead.


Twenty-Five hundred soldiers of the
regular army, in full dress array, gra-
ciously acted as an escort to the Wis
iting men of the sea and were literally
applauded. Rear Admiral Evans, COM
manding the fleets, and the six other
rear admirals in command of squad
rons and divisions rode in carriages.

One of the most beautiful bird stories
ever told by writer or scientist was
acted out by two carrier pigeons at
grocery store on Court and Hill streets
last week.


The owner of the store was presented
with the two pigeons, one black and
one white.


The first day he had them he let them
out of the coop, and they circled
around the house a few times and flew
away. That night they returned and
settled in their coop as though they
had been there always.


Next day the owner let them loose
again, when the birds flew away. That
night however, but one of them re-
turned, the black one. Disconsolate 1t
went to the cot and the first thing
when released the following morning
1t began it's untiring search for its mate.
The pigeon flew around the house,
coming through at the front as soon
as the door was opened, searching
every room and beating with it's wings
against the back door until that was
opened for it. Then it sped away In
quest of the missing mate.
All that day 1t kept returning to the
cote to see II its mate had returned.
Not finding the lost one. 1t would wing
it's way again over the great city.
Time and again this was repeated until
the day was closed.


When released the following morning
1t took up the search Immediately, its
black body flashing over the tree tops
on the crest of the hill where the store
containing the cote is located. A


Not long afterward the black car
rier was seen approaching the building
again, but its flight was not alone. For
near it, with, steadily beating pinions,
the white mate shone like new found
pearl In contrast to the sable plumage
of it's mate.


And that night as the owner went to
close the dove COTE he found the two
carrier pigeons, the black and the
white, nestled together in the cote. The
lost had been found, and the quest OF
the faithful carrier had been rewarded
with success after days of earnest
searching.

Special Dispatch to The Star.


NEW YORK, December 2-Territic
storms were encountered by the Fabre
line steamship Madonna, which arrived
today from Naples and Marseille.


The vessel encountered three storms of
cyclonic character. Five of her crew
were injured when a great wave in the
Mediterranean swept the vessel.


In subsequent hurricanes deck fittings
were swept away, heavy headlights and
doors broken and passengers cabins
flooded. Staterooms on the starboard side
of the vessel were almost completely
sutted.


There were only a score of cabin pas
sengers on board. Several lost clothing
and effects. They We're driven from thei,
rooms to the saloon for shelter.


Capt. Pavy of the liner said the storms
were the worst Of his experience At
times the ship seemed submerged, he said.


A revolving storm of great violence
struck the liner last Saturday. For
hours She was swept by tremendous seas.
The passengers remained in their berths
throughout the day.


She sailed from Naples December 8,
and was fifteen days making the passage


December 90 the steamship ran into a
terrific northeaster, in which the seas
were frightful. They tumbled aboard on
the. forward deck and swept along the
starboard side. smashing everything in
their progress.


Heavy headlight glass Of the cabin port
holes was broken out and smashed into
fragments. The wooden panel doors lead
ing to the deck from the cabins were
broken out and carried away. The iron
rails. stanchiors and heavy teakwood rails
were broken out in several pa ccs.


At O'Clock In the morning, when the
first big seas smashed into the state
rooms. portfolios and doors. the water
flooding the cabins, drove all passengers
into the saloons in their night clothes On
their return to their rooms they found
themselves destitute of clothing.


Capt Pavy was OBLIGED to exc out their
wants from his wardrobe. He supplied
one woman passenger with some of his
heavy stockings and big sea boots and
storm coat until better provisions could
be made.


This last storm was cyclonic and of
great force, the center moving to the
northeast. The ships doctor. said the
water entered his room so quickly that
he was Obliged to swim about until it
swept out again. The Madonna brought
SAT steerage passengers.

WEST PLAINS, Mo-, Sept. 2O.-John
Roberts and his wife today resisted a
sheriff's posse in a desperate battle near
Prestonia, one mile south of the Mis-
souri, Kansas line, when the officers
attempted to arrest Roberts for the
killing of B. e. Kessinger, a neighbor,
last night.


AS a result, two men and Sheriff
Mooney of Baxter county. Arkansas.
are mortally wounded Roberts and
two members of the posse, Max T..
Lowery AND his son, are all seriously
hurt.


Roberts may not survive.


The murder of Kessinger, it is said
was cold blooded. Roberts went tQ
the house late in the evening and
called his victim to the door. When
Kessinger appeared Roberts fred de-
liberately and killed him.


The cause of the murder has not
been learned here.


Organizes Posse


Sheriff Mooney collected several
deputies when he was informed of the
crime early this morning, and started
to arrest Roberts.


The posse was hailed by the woman
and told to keep away, but when the
sheriff continued to advance both she
and her husband opened fire.


Mooney was shot by the woman. HIS
fall disconnected his deputies for few
minutes, and Roberts and his wife
took advantage of this to barricade the
house. They defended the building for
hours.


When the firing from within the
house ceased the door was broken
down.


Mrs. Roberts, suffering from four
teen wounds, was dying and her con-
dition was such that no attempt was
made to remove her to Jail.


Roberts and the wounded officers
were taken to Mountain Home, Ark.

ernor-elect, reported TO Judge Morris

dered them back to the jury room.


This is Caleb Powers fourth trial.
His first trial took place in 1900. when
The jury. after thirty minutes delibera-
ton. found him guilty and fixed his
punishment at life imprisonment; the

dict being reversed by the court or

that the case had been heard before
partisan juries and therefore in viola

the federal constitution, guaranteeing
every man a fair trial. The third
trial, in August. 1903. resulted in con-
viction. Powers this time was SEN
fenced to death on the gaiiows, but
again the case was appealed and re-
yersed

ing his imprisonment. He has been

nope and expecting acquittal in the

MANILA. October 5.-The Atlantic bat
can which swept Manila bay for twelve
hours and did much damage ashore.


Typhoon signals were displayed early
Sunday morning. but the storm broke
over the bay suddenly and unexpectedly
at noon. 1t was impossible to hoist the
cutters and launches belonging to the
feet because Of the danger of smashing
them against the steel sides Of the battle
ships, and the little craft were sent sour
rying inside The breakwater into the Pasig
river. where they remained oil night
The storm quickly increased in intensity.
and the torrential rains shut in the ships.


At o'clock Sunday night the storm had
reached its height. and 1t then gradually
tapered down until at midnight It was
comparatively calm. although heavy seas
swung across the harbor.


During the storm all the battleships ad
steam up ready for any emergency.


Sperry Issues Orders.


Rear Admiral Sperry finally ordered the
flagship Connecticut and the Kansas. Min
nesota. Vermont, Virginia and Ohio under
way. They were close to the breakwater
and Admiral Sperry feared they might
drag anchors. The six vessels steamed
down close to Cavite, where they
anchored.


At times the wind blew at the rate OF
100 miles an hour. All communication
with shore was cut off. 1t was impos-
sible during the height of the storm to
see the warships through the haze Of rain
and spray. On shore it was dangerous &c
go about Several carriages were over
turned by the wind. trees were blown
down. electric wires were Frustrated and
several buildings were unroofed. Among
the buildings unroofed was the depot OF
the commissary. Several naval officers
ashore on various errands were compelled
to remain ashore all night.

ship Vermont. died Saturday.

violation of the prohibition ordinance

ten, for the defense, interposed the OBJ
jections that there was insufficient evil
dence, that the court had no jurisdic-

by the charter. The objections were
overruled and Chief Williams, Capt.
McCord, Sergeant Philnps and PATROL
man Gallemore were put on the stand
and told the story of the raid.


Attorney Jutten made a plea for
leniency. City Attorney Long said
that there was no special reason, that
he could see, for leniency. He stated

Lawson then imposed the fine, which
